Doubt-driven review · 26 August 2026

When does the body reach the mind during sleep?

A complete, sourced, adversarial review of the Bial Foundation application on infraslow brain rhythms and the conscious registration of nocturnal hot flashes. Twenty agents, 197 raw findings, every one put to a refuter whose job was to prove it wrong.

The deadline is 31 August 2026 — five days. Maximum grant €60,000; 2024/25 round funded 80 of 432 applications (19%). The document currently contains no principal investigator, host entity, CVs, budget, schedule or ethics reference. The words “host”, “budget” and “2027” do not appear in it.

The verdict

A strong idea attached to an instrument that cannot make the measurement

Not fundable as written, and the reasons are structural rather than editorial. The idea is genuinely original and squarely psychophysiological: substitute an endogenous, frequent, peripherally measurable interoceptive event for the experimenter's tone, and ask whether an infraslow brain rhythm decides which such events are noticed. But the confirmatory instrument cannot answer it in either direction. A positive result is manufactured by the design — a zero-phase filter estimates the predictor from EEG recorded after the outcome, and the outcome is defined by a change in the same signal — and a null is uninterpretable, because there is no positive control, no bounded onset error, and the predictor's measurability at frontopolar derivations is contradicted by both papers cited as feasibility support. Underneath that, the application contains no expected event count, no effect size and no power figure, and its single quantitative power claim is arithmetically the reverse of how jitter acts; on the review's own yield model the design is short by roughly an order of magnitude for any effect size comparable to published phase-gating magnitudes. Finally, the 222-woman "cohort" is an undisclosed four-arm randomised trial of hormone therapy and CBT-I in women meeting a clinical insomnia threshold, the analysed timepoint is never named, and the primary outcome measure does not appear in that trial's approved protocol — so the reviewer discovers from the applicants' own reference list both the eligibility question and the possibility that the outcome variable does not yet exist in the data. All four panellists recommend revise and resubmit; so do I, and what is required is a redesign plus pilot numbers, not a rewrite.

Where they agreed and where they split

Unanimous on the shape of the problem and on the recommendation. All four score sheets read identically in direction: significance and innovation at the strong end (2-4), approach and feasibility at the weak end (7-8), team 4-5, fit 5-6, overall 7 in every case, revise and resubmit from all four. The spread between innovation and approach is the whole review — a strong idea attached to an instrument that cannot make the measurement. Four independent convergences carry the most weight, because the reviewers reached them by different routes. Every reviewer concluded that a POSITIVE result would be uninterpretable: the neurophysiologist and the statistician via the non-causal filter, the consciousness reviewer via the press outcome, the clinician via unbounded onset error. All four flagged the absent power arithmetic. All four flagged the undisclosed nesting inside the MHT/CBT-I trial. Three of four independently reached the same conclusion about the inverted confirmatory hierarchy. Where they genuinely split, and who is right: (1) What should be primary. The statistician and the neurophysiologist want the hierarchy inverted so cortical arousal is primary, on the ground that it carries roughly thirteen times the information at the same event count. The consciousness reviewer resists this in substance: arousal-primary is a replication of Lecci et al. with a spontaneous rather than a delivered event, teaches nothing about conscious access, and so weakens rather than strengthens the fit to Bial's remit. Both are right about different things, and the fix must satisfy both: invert the hierarchy for what is estimable at this yield AND add a no-report cortical outcome (a flash-locked evoked response and a flash-locked change in the heartbeat evoked potential, following the draft's own cited Cataldi et al.) as a third rung. Inverting without the third rung leaves a well-powered replication; adding the third rung without inverting leaves an underpowered claim. The consciousness reviewer is right that this is the change that decides whether the project belongs in this competition, and it is cheap because it uses recordings already made — though frontal-only EEG with no EOG limits it, so it must be presented as an exploratory rung and a feasibility outcome, not as a solved measure. (2) Whether the frontal montage is fatal or revisable. The neurophysiologist calls it fatal; the other three call it major. The neurophysiologist is right and is the domain authority: the evidence is one-directional (Lazar reports frontopolar lowest of any region, Lecci recorded C3/C4, Dimitriades locates the peak centro-parietally), and the draft's stated fallback is computed from the same failing signal. This is not fixable by writing. Either a central derivation is added, or the primary aim is demoted. (3) Whether the Article 16(6) therapy exclusion is decisive. The clinician says it is arguable and that the real problem is candour rather than scope; the verified findings support that, noting that Bial's own funded portfolio includes clinically adjacent work. The clinician is right. The exclusion is a high-probability screening risk that the draft simply fails to argue, and the damage is done by non-disclosure rather than by the nesting itself. (4) Form compliance. All four treat it as minor or moderate. On the regulation they are all wrong on one item: the absence of a designated Host Entity is an eligibility bar under Art. 16(7), not a scoring deduction, so it outranks every scientific objection in the fix order despite being the cheapest thing in the document to fix. That collective under-weighting is the most dangerous blind spot in the four reviews. One further point no reviewer made forcefully enough: the clinician's proposal to screen on measured nocturnal flash rate rather than on self-reported symptom interference is the cleanest single improvement in the entire panel. It removes a selection criterion that is the very measure whose unreliability is the proposal's premise, and it aligns the analysis sample with what the analysis actually needs. Adopt it.

Each reviewer in full

Sleep neurophysiologist — revise and resubmit, overall 7

Summary

This is a good question attached to a measurement that, as specified, cannot be made. The conceptual move is genuinely original and I want it to succeed: use a spontaneous, frequent, peripherally measurable interoceptive event to test infraslow gating, which escapes the stimulus-randomisation design that the whole arousability literature is built on, and delivers the one cell no delivered stimulus can — the quiet event with neither arousal nor report. I would fund that idea. I cannot fund this instrument. Three defects are, in my judgement, disqualifying as written. First, the predictor is estimated from the one scalp location where the phenomenon is known to be weakest: the infraslow sigma fluctuation is centro-parietal, and Lazar et al. (2019) — cited in the draft *as feasibility support* — reports that frontopolar sites have significantly lower integrated infraslow power than every other region, with parietal highest; Lecci's human recordings were C3/C4 and Carro-Domínguez et al. (2025) measured sigma at Cz. The ZMax gives F7-Fpz and F8-Fpz. The fallback for weak frontal expression is the amplitude of the same frontal signal, which inherits the failure it is meant to escape. Second, the phase estimate is non-causal. A zero-phase band-pass at 0.01-0.04 Hz has support of tens of seconds on both sides of the onset sample, so post-onset EEG determines "phase at onset" — and post-onset EEG is exactly where a registered or aroused flash produces spindle loss, movement and muscle artefact, on two frontal derivations with no EOG or EMG, with the arousal-scoring band (>16 Hz) abutting the predictor band (11-16 Hz). That single choice manufactures an association between "fragility at onset" and registration with zero true gating, in precisely the predicted direction. The draft's long circularity discussion is about the flash detector and never touches this, which is the larger circularity by far. Third, onset timing. The draft correctly names a ~12 s tolerance as its own dealbreaker and then supplies no evidence that any link in the chain achieves it: the cited detector emits a decision every 15 s, computes features over ±250 s and ±500 s windows, and was scored against expert annotations within a ±90 s matching window — seven times the budget — against a gold standard rule defined on a 30 s rise. The proposed precision check (dispersion of intervals between peripheral markers) measures agreement between two effectors, not error against the central event, and is entirely blind to systematic lag, which rotates rather than shrinks the estimate at 7.2° per second. Beyond these: the directional prediction is probably inverted, and the draft's own named collaborator is second author on the human paper that contradicts it (Dimitriades et al. 2026, n=154: microarousals cluster at the ISFS *peak*, p<0.0001 in every age group); "fragility = low sigma power" misreads Lecci and Osorio-Forero, both of whom define the arousable phase by the sigma *derivative*. The inclusion criterion that governs the entire analysis sample ("stable NREM") is never defined, and its relaxed fallback (two cycles, ~100 s) is shorter than the one-cycle period of the passband's own low edge and less than half the ≥256-280 s minimum both published human ISF studies require. There is no event count anywhere in the document, and the single quantitative power claim is mathematically backwards. The confirmatory test is the least informative of the three analyses proposed and cannot demonstrate the advertised claim. And the cohort is an undisclosed four-arm randomised trial of hormone therapy and CBT-I in women with ISI≥10, described as "physically healthy", studied "without intervention", with a primary outcome measure (the button press) that does not appear in the parent protocol at all.

Objections raised

  • Major This sentence cites, as feasibility support, the paper that reports the opposite. Lazar, Dijk & Lazar (2019) state that the frontopolar region had significantly lower integrated infraslow power than all other brain regions, and that the parietal region had significantly higher power than all others; their summary is that these oscillations are most prominent centro-parieto-occipitally. Lecci's human recordings were C3 and C4. Carro-Domínguez et al. (2025, Nat Commun) measured sigma at Cz. Dimitriades et al. (2026, n=154) place peak-frequency and area-under-curve extrema in central regions. The ZMax records F7-Fpz and F8-Fpz — bilateral frontopolar, referenced to Fpz — which is the single worst montage on the head for this signal, and the study has no other EEG. Separately, the bias statistic quoted is close to irrelevant: a mean bias in relative sigma bandpower is a static offset, and a constant offset in the log envelope is removed by the 0.01-0.04 Hz band-pass entirely. What matters is whether the 0.02 Hz modulation of the envelope survives two frontal derivations with wearable noise, and that validation reports no time-resolved spectral analysis at all. Gamma also has a smaller bias than sigma in the same list, so 'smallest bias of any band' is not even true. I would not accept 'frontal expression is itself a feasibility outcome' as an answer when the answer is already in the literature and is unfavourable — and the stated fallback for weak frontal expression is the amplitude of the same weak frontal signal.
    Feasibility is supported: sigma-band power from this headband shows the smallest bias of any band against polysomnography (0.005 ± 0.012; Esfahani et al., 2023), and the infraslow modulation of sigma is established in humans (Lecci et al., 2017; Lazar et al., 2019). [DRAFT.md L271-274]
  • Major Zero-phase filtering is non-causal. A filtfilt at 0.01-0.04 Hz has an effective impulse response spanning tens of seconds on both sides of any sample, so the phase you assign to flash onset is partly determined by EEG recorded after that onset. Now consider what the outcomes do to post-onset EEG. A registered flash means the woman woke enough to locate and press a wristband button; an aroused flash means, by the draft's own scoring rule, a transient in the band immediately adjacent to the predictor band. Both produce spindle suppression, both produce movement, and on frontopolar derivations with no EOG and no chin EMG both produce muscle and eye artefact that lands squarely in 11-16 Hz. That post-onset sigma drop propagates backwards through the non-causal filter into the estimated onset phase and pulls it toward low sigma — which the draft labels fragility, and which the draft predicts should be associated with registration. The design therefore manufactures its own hypothesised result with zero true gating. This is not a subtle bias: against a 50 s cycle a few seconds of leakage is tens of degrees. The draft devotes eight lines to circularity in the flash detector (L246-254) and never mentions this, which is the far larger circularity. Fix: estimate phase causally from a pre-onset window only, with a stated guard interval, quantify the causal estimator's error on flash-free segments, and add a hard negative control — recompute the primary model with phase taken from a matched epoch one full cycle earlier, where a true gating effect must vanish and an artefact will not. Also move the predictor band away from the arousal band, and have arousals scored by a rater who cannot see the sigma envelope.
    Instantaneous ISF phase is obtained from the log sigma envelope by zero-phase band-pass filtering (0.01-0.04 Hz, empirical peak reported per participant) and the Hilbert transform to calculate the IAF phase. [DRAFT.md L267-269]
  • Major The draft names its own kill criterion — a quarter of a 50 s cycle, about 12 s — and then presents no evidence that any link in the chain reaches it. I have recorded thousands of nights and I do not believe sudomotor onset can be localised to seconds from the wrist. Look at what the cited detector actually does: it emits a binary decision every 15 s; its skin-conductance feature designates onset as the ±2 minutes around a predicted onset; its temperature feature averages over the prior and following 500 s; its PPG feature differences heart rate 120 s before against 120 s after; and it was evaluated against expert annotations using a ±90 s matching window. Ninety seconds is nearly two full cycles — more than 640° of phase. The field's gold-standard event rule is itself a 2 µS rise within a 30 s period, so the reference standard is 30 s grained. Change-point back-dating on the electrodermal inflection is a sensible idea, but it is an untested one: no source in the proposal reports its precision against any reference, and the draft's proposed check measures the wrong thing. The dispersion of intervals between the electrodermal, temperature and pulse-rate markers quantifies agreement among three peripheral effectors. It cannot see any error common to all of them — sudomotor conduction delay, sweat-gland response latency, wrist-versus-sternal propagation — and it is entirely blind to systematic lag. Systematic lag is the error mode that destroys this study, because it rotates the estimated preferred phase rather than shrinking it: at a 50 s cycle, 7.2° per second, so a 12 s back-dating bias moves a trough onto a flank and 25 s inverts the label. The direction the Expected Outcomes section commits to is therefore not recoverable unless bias is bounded to a few seconds, and nothing here bounds it. This needs a laboratory validation night with simultaneous sternal skin conductance as the reference, reporting the bias and SD of back-dated onset error, and it needs to be a gate on the confirmatory analysis, not a deliverable of it.
    Because the ISF cycle is only about 50 s, onset uncertainty translates directly into phase uncertainty... Intervals between this inflection and the accompanying temperature and pulse-rate changes index achievable precision. [DRAFT.md L258-263]
  • Major This is a misreading of the source papers, and the human data point the other way. Lecci et al. define the two phases by the sigma derivative, not the level: wake-ups and sleep-throughs occurred during declining and rising sigma power respectively. Osorio-Forero et al. (2021), in the file supplied, targeted high or low arousability by detecting online 'whether sigma power started to rise or decline', and report that noradrenaline 'had already declined when sigma levels started rising, producing a non-symmetrical U-shaped time course' — so the high-noradrenaline, high-arousability window sits at and just after the sigma peak, not in the trough. Level and slope are 90° apart. The human evidence is worse for this prediction than the rodent evidence is. Dimitriades et al. (2026, Sci Rep, n=154, ages 8-26) report that the highest percentage of microarousals occurred around the ISFS peak compared with phase bins in the negative half wave, in children (p<0.0001), early adolescents (p=0.028), late adolescents (p<0.0001) and young adults (p<0.0001). Carro-Domínguez et al. (2025, Nat Commun) report heart rate significantly higher at the sigma peak than during rise or fall, and note explicitly that this is unlike mice. Two things follow. Scientifically, the pre-registered direction is probably inverted; the sin/cos test survives but the narrative and the Expected Outcomes commitment do not. Presentationally, this is worse: Osorio-Forero is second author on the Dimitriades paper, and the draft claims him as team expertise (L58-61) while citing neither that paper nor its result. A Board member who knows this literature — and several of us do — will conclude that the applicants have not read the human work on their own predictor. Cite it, and use it to justify a genuinely two-sided test.
    Extending the exogenous literature, flashes arriving in fragility (low sigma power) are predicted to be more likely registered, and followed by an arousal, than those in continuity. [DRAFT.md L355-357]
  • Major This one clause governs the entire analysis sample and it is defined nowhere in Data processing or Statistical analyses. The only quantity appears seventy lines later, in the contingency section, as 'three ISF cycles' relaxed to two — and the draft never says whether the bout is measured before onset, after onset, or symmetrically around it. That choice is decisive, and the non-causal filter makes the centred reading the natural one. If stability must hold after onset, then any flash that produces an arousal, a stage shift or an awakening terminates its own bout and is excluded, so inclusion is conditioned on the negation of both outcomes and the study systematically deletes the events that carry the effect. The base rates make this bite hard rather than incidentally: in the review the draft itself relies on, 70% of nocturnal flashes were associated with an arousal from sleep and only 20% occurred without disturbance to sleep; in the GnRH-agonist model study reported in the same review, flashes occurred primarily in association with stage N1 (20%) and wake epochs (51%), leaving under a third for consolidated NREM before any bout criterion is applied. Then the relaxed fallback breaks the predictor rather than weakening it. Two cycles at 0.02 Hz is 100 s, which is exactly one period of the passband's own 0.01 Hz low edge, and filtfilt edge transients consume a large fraction of a segment that short. Both published human ISF studies set their minimum far higher and say why: Lazar et al. required ≥256 s contiguous intervals; Dimitriades et al. required ≥280 s continuous N2, 'chosen to ensure two full cycles of the lowest frequency of interest (0.0075 Hz)'. And these are women with an Insomnia Severity Index of 10 or above, in whom long uninterrupted N2 bouts are by definition scarce. Define the criterion, make it pre-onset only, set it at ≥280 s, state the edge-discard rule and the minimum distance an includable onset must sit inside the bout, and meet low yield with more nights rather than a shorter window.
    Analyses are restricted to stable (and non-artifactual) NREM. [DRAFT.md L270] ... Low event yield is met by relaxing the stable-bout criterion from three ISF cycles to two, pre-specified as secondary. [DRAFT.md L343-345]
  • Major The one quantitative statement in the power section is mathematically wrong, and it is the statement that licenses stating no event count at all. Independent onset jitter attenuates a circular effect multiplicatively — for wrapped-normal error of SD σ against period T the first harmonic is scaled by exp(-(2πσ/T)²/2) — so the estimator stays consistent, power is strictly increasing in N at every jitter level, and there is no threshold beyond which additional events stop helping. What jitter does is inflate the required N by the reciprocal of that factor squared: about 1.5-fold at 5 s, 4-fold at 9.4 s, roughly 12-fold at the draft's own quarter-cycle. That is a strong argument for precision; it is not an argument that count is unconstrained. As written, the draft contradicts itself — L191-192 justifies four nights precisely because 'power depends on event count' — and then, having declared count non-binding, states no expected number of analysable flashes anywhere in 464 lines. Six sequential exclusions are named at L204-206 and not one retention rate is given; the tense also slides between 'simulation shows' (done) and 'Simulations use the observed counts and precision' (only possible after the money is spent). I am being asked to fund a confirmatory test whose detectability the applicants agree is unknown. Give me the yield table with a rate and a source at every step, the expected registered and aroused subsets, and a power curve over that count crossed with a jitter grid for a named minimum effect of interest — and note that the only published anchor for phase gating of conscious detection is modest (circular R ≈ 0.34 for cardiac and respiratory modulation of near-threshold tactile detection in wakefulness), so the effect you are hunting is small.
    The binding constraint is measurement precision rather than event count: onset jitter translates directly into phase uncertainty against a 50-s cycle, and simulation shows power ceasing to improve with additional events once jitter exceeds a quarter of the cycle. [DRAFT.md L315-318]
  • Major The proposal nominates as confirmatory the analysis that cannot demonstrate its own claim, and designates as exploratory the only one that can. Decompose it: P(registered | phase) = P(aroused | phase) × P(registered | aroused, phase). The draft concedes at L299-302 that a button press requires sufficient arousal and that registered flashes will be largely a subset of aroused ones. So if the first factor carries the effect, a significant primary result is a replication of phase-dependent arousability — which Lecci et al. published in 2017 — obtained with a spontaneous rather than a delivered event. Interesting, but not the advertised finding, which is that phase gates access to reportable awareness over and above arousability. The term that isolates that is the second factor, registration among aroused flashes, and it is explicitly non-confirmatory. There is also no stated test for the comparison the Summary promises at L54-56: 'comparing the two' names no estimand, no statistic and no decision rule, and informally eyeballing two sin/cos coefficient pairs fitted to nested outcomes is not a test of additional modulation. Compounding it, the draft refuses to adjust for flash magnitude on mediator grounds at L306-308 and then conditions on arousal — equally a post-onset mediator, and by its own account nearly necessary for the outcome — at L301-302. Pick one principle. My recommendation: make the arousal model primary, since it carries far more information at the same event count, and make registration-among-aroused the co-primary that isolates conscious access, with the decomposition stated as direct and indirect effects in a mediation model and the assumptions each requires spelled out.
    The primary registration model is confirmatory; all else is exploratory. [DRAFT.md L310-311]
  • Major Neither sentence is true of the cohort the draft's own reference list identifies, and the non-disclosure is the part that will cost you. The only plausible referent for '222 perimenopausal women' is the applicants' own listed protocol (L449-454): a four-arm two-by-two randomised trial of menopausal hormone therapy and online cognitive behavioural and circadian therapy for insomnia, enrolling on an Insomnia Severity Index of 10 or higher, with transdermal estradiol plus oral progesterone in two of the four arms and device recordings at three timepoints. So: half the sample takes hormone-altering medication by design, at exactly the timepoints when the recordings are made; the draft's own cited review reports that hormone therapy reduces hot flash frequency by around 75%, meaning the intervention removes the events the study is powered on; the CBT-I arms perturb sleep continuity, spindle expression and arousal threshold, which is the predictor; and 'physically healthy' is a description of a clinical insomnia population. The draft never states which timepoint supplies the analysed nights. If the answer is baseline only — which is the only answer compatible with L369-370 — then say so plainly, and recompute the yield on one four-night block per woman rather than three. Two further consequences. 222 is a recruitment target inclusive of a dropout allowance, not a set of women with data; the draft says they are 'already being recorded' and then reveals five lines later that 65 have been screened, so the 137-woman analysis sample is a projection resting on a projection. And Bial excludes 'projects involving clinical or experimental models of human disease and therapy' — a defensible case can be made that a non-interventional analysis of pre-randomisation recordings of a normal physiological event falls outside that, but the draft makes no such case, because it does not disclose the trial. A reviewer who discovers the RCT from your own reference list has stopped assessing the science and started assessing the candour.
    They are physically healthy and take no hormone-altering medication [DRAFT.md L199-200] ... in healthy humans and without intervention [DRAFT.md L369-370]
  • Major The primary outcome variable does not appear in the parent protocol. That protocol specifies objective flash estimation from the wristband, questionnaires and a consensus sleep diary; it contains no nocturnal button press, no event marker, and no five-tap synchronisation procedure. So the measure on which the confirmatory analysis depends does not exist in the data the draft describes as 'already being recorded', and cannot exist for any participant enrolled before an approved amendment. Adding a participant-facing nocturnal task to an approved interventional protocol is a substantive change requiring an ethics amendment and re-consent, and the draft asserts blanket approval for 'the study' while leaving the reference as a literal placeholder — against a regulation that requires documentary evidence of submission at application and no signed Agreement without the approval document. Beyond governance, the measure itself is unvalidated as an index of awareness and is not the same instrument as the 1.5-flashes-reported figure the Summary leans on, which is a retrospective morning count. A press is a conjunction of interoceptive access, arousal sufficient for volitional action, correct causal attribution of the bodily state to a flash, motor execution and compliance — and only the first is the construct. There is also no operational definition anywhere: no window linking a press to an onset (a flash lasts one to five minutes and orienting time will itself vary with sleep depth, which is the predictor), no rule for presses with no nearby detected flash, no rule for two flashes in one window, no handling of presses during scored wake when the analysis is restricted to stable NREM. Different defensible windows will give different confirmatory results from the same data. And nobody has asked whether instructing women to monitor for flashes changes the flashes — you have three wristband-only nights against four EEG nights, which is a free within-participant reactivity control you are not using.
    On EEG nights participants press a wristband button as soon as they think they are having a flash; this time-stamped press is a prospective measure of conscious registration. [DRAFT.md L215-217]
  • Moderate Four things are wrong in these two clauses and the source file supplied with this application says so. The sensors were not a research-grade wristband: they were a customised array of consumer-grade commercially available components — a Grove skin-conductance sensor at 64 Hz, a TI temperature sensor at 16 Hz, a SparkFun PPG at 512 Hz, an NXP accelerometer — taped to the wrist and wired into a Compumedics PSG amplifier through a digital-to-analog output card. The paper's own framing is that no consumer-space solution exists and that it shows 'initial feasibility'. It is not the EmbracePlus, which differs in sensors, placement, sampling and signal conditioning, and whose manufacturer publishes no EDA accuracy figure against a criterion defined as a 2 µS rise in 30 s. The sample was three women, mean age 55.6, who had undergone natural menopause — postmenopausal, not the perimenopausal population here — contributing 27 flashes in a single ~12 h session in sound-attenuated, temperature-controlled bedrooms. The quoted operating point was obtained by randomly splitting 15 s frames 80/20 across only three participants, so training and test folds necessarily share subjects and share individual flashes: that is leakage, not subject-wise validation, and none is possible at n=3. And the class was oversampled to 1:2, so the specificity figure describes performance at roughly 33% prevalence rather than the ~3% of a real night. At overnight prevalence the missing number is positive predictive value, and it matters here more than usual: a false positive cannot be registered and carries no flash-related arousal, so false positives accumulate exactly in the quiet-flash cell that carries the hypothesis, and because the detector's cardiac and electrodermal inputs are themselves coupled to the infraslow rhythm, phase-dependent false alarms would mimic the predicted effect. The draft's own cited review places this class of method 'mostly in the development phase' and notes it has 'not been applied to track hot flashes in clinical trials' — written by a co-author of the detector paper. Report the provenance honestly, make detector re-derivation and validation on your own hardware against sternal skin conductance a costed work package with a pass criterion, and add blinded manual adjudication of every candidate event.
    Flashes are detected from multi-sensor features of a research-grade wristband (Tsiartas et al., 2021). [DRAFT.md L65-66] ... reaching over 90% sensitivity at 95.6% specificity against expert-scored sternal skin conductance [DRAFT.md L244-245]
  • Moderate Before asking what phase an event arrived at, establish that there is an oscillation to have a phase. Chen et al. (2025, PNAS, n=1,025) tested exactly this and report that short-term (<15 s) patterns of past spindle history are the main determinant of spindle timing, accounting for over 70% of the statistical deviance — exceeding cortical up/down state, sleep depth, and long-term history from 15 to 90 s including ~50 s infraslow activity. The draft does not cite it. That matters because a band-pass plus Hilbert transform will return an instantaneous phase from a point-process-driven envelope whether or not a narrowband oscillation is present: the filter manufactures one. Two further specifics. A 0.01-0.04 Hz passband has a bandwidth of 0.03 Hz on a centre of 0.025 Hz — fractional bandwidth 1.2, which is not narrowband by any definition, so the Bedrosian condition underlying the analytic-signal construction is grossly violated; and the sigma envelope is known to be non-sinusoidal, since your own collaborator's paper reports a 'non-symmetrical U-shaped time course'. Note also that nobody in the human field does what this draft proposes: Lazar et al. (2019) used spectral methods and estimated no phase at all; Dimitriades et al. low-pass filtered at 0.04 Hz and binned by detected peaks, troughs and zero-crossings into eight bins; Osorio-Forero et al. classified cycles online as rising or declining. Adopt the operationalisation your own group validated — detect cycles on the envelope and classify onsets by cycle position or limb — narrow the band around each participant's empirical peak rather than merely reporting it, require the observed peak to exceed interval-shuffled surrogates that preserve spindle count and individual refractoriness before phase is treated as meaningful, and report per-event phase uncertainty with unidentifiable events excluded.
    the infraslow modulation of sigma is established in humans (Lecci et al., 2017; Lazar et al., 2019) [DRAFT.md L273-274]
  • Moderate Two problems, one of which I would raise even in a strong application. First, the criterion is not the standard one and is attributed to the wrong source. The AASM rule is an abrupt shift in EEG frequency including alpha, theta and/or frequencies above 16 Hz but explicitly excluding spindles, lasting at least 3 s, preceded by at least 10 s of continuous sleep, with no upper bound, and in REM additionally requiring a concurrent submental EMG rise. The draft keeps only the >16 Hz clause, imposes a 15 s ceiling that is not an AASM criterion, drops the preceding-sleep rule, and — in a study whose predictor is 11-16 Hz sigma power — drops the spindle exclusion. It cites a substantive research paper rather than the scoring manual for a scoring rule. The ZMax carries no EOG and no chin EMG, so neither AASM staging nor AASM arousal scoring is achievable, which is worth stating plainly since it is the honest justification for excluding REM. Frontal-only recording makes it worse: eye movements and frontalis EMG generate precisely the high-frequency transients that mimic arousals, and a hot flash generates movement, so the supporting outcome is measured on a channel the event itself contaminates. Second, and this is the omission I find hardest to excuse: the word 'blind' does not appear anywhere in this document. A human scorer marking ambiguous frontal transients, who can see the wristband channels, the flash detections or the button presses, will score more arousals near known flashes. That single unblinded judgement can produce the supporting result on its own and, because the outcomes are near-nested, contaminate the primary one. State that scoring is performed on recordings stripped of all wristband and press markers, completed and locked before the merge, with the merge done by someone else, and report inter-rater agreement for arousals separately from staging.
    Recordings are scored in 30-s epochs (wake, REM, N1-N3) by an experienced scorer... Arousals follow standard criteria: transient > 16 Hz activity lasting 3-15 s (Wassing et al., 2019). [DRAFT.md L234-237]
  • Moderate This substitution is presented as robustness and is in fact a change of question, and it is the only insurance the proposal carries against the risk it identifies as principal. Phase and amplitude are close to orthogonal here. The hypothesis is about when within a cycle an event arrives, and the reason the design is interesting is that phase is roughly orthogonal to mean sleep depth within a bout. Pre-flash amplitude is a state-level quantity, ambiguous between two constructs the draft never separates — the modulation depth of the rhythm over the preceding window, and the instantaneous sigma level before onset — and both are heavily confounded with N2 versus N3, spindle density, homeostatic pressure and time of night, which is the confound the phase design exists to escape. The same amplitude also occurs twice per cycle, once rising and once falling, and the rodent work manipulated arousability precisely by targeting rising versus declining sigma, so an amplitude predictor averages over the two states the hypothesis is about. A null on amplitude is compatible with strong phase gating, and vice versa. The stated reason it 'tolerates far more timing error' is that it discards the temporal information the hypothesis concerns; that is a symptom, not a virtue. The second trigger is self-defeating, as noted: if frontal ISF expression is too weak for reliable phase, it is too weak for meaningful amplitude, because both come off the same frontopolar envelope. And every threshold governing the switch is absent — no value for marker dispersion, no criterion for 'weak frontal expression', no trigger count for low yield, no compliance floor. A pre-registration whose decision rules are described but not stated gives full post hoc latitude. Replace the fallback with one that preserves the phase claim while tolerating jitter — the sign of the sigma derivative at onset, or coarse cycle-position bins with onset error propagated as measurement error — and keep amplitude as an honestly labelled separate secondary question.
    the primary predictor switches from ISF phase to pre-flash ISF amplitude, which tolerates far more timing error while testing the same hypothesis; weak frontal ISF expression triggers the same rule. [DRAFT.md L341-343]
  • Moderate Two synchronisation anchors per night, and the citation offered does not support the method. Sikder et al. built an automatic accelerometer cross-correlation and then abandoned it: they state they opted to synchronise manually by visual inspection of the raw tri-axial accelerometer data because the manual outcome was more reliable. They aligned ZMax to PSG, not ZMax to a wristband; they used the Empatica E4, not the EmbracePlus; they recorded one night per participant, so the paper establishes nothing about mid-night drift stability; they note the devices lack a reliable internal clock; and they report no residual synchronisation error in seconds. PPG was not used for alignment at all, and an independent 2026 concurrent-PSG analysis of that same dataset found wrist PPG-derived HRV usable in under half of epochs — so cross-correlating heart-rate series is the weakest of the available channels. Meanwhile a fixed offset plus a single linear drift term, anchored only at lights-off and on waking, cannot detect mid-night non-linearity, sample-rate jitter or dropped samples, and mid-night is where the events are. Against a 50 s cycle this is not a rounding error: a 2 s synchronisation SD alone costs a few per cent of effect, and it combines in quadrature with an onset-timing error that is itself unbounded. Cite the manual procedure as what it is, add mid-night markers so drift is estimated from more than two anchors, pre-specify a maximum acceptable tap-to-tap residual beyond which a night is excluded, and put the residual distribution in the error budget as a number rather than a promise to report.
    EEG and wristband are synchronised by cross-correlating accelerometer and PPG signals (Sikder et al., 2026), with a fixed offset and linear drift estimated per recording; tap markers validate this and residual error is reported. [DRAFT.md L227-230]
  • Moderate There is no positive control, so half the outcome space is uninterpretable. If phase does not predict registration, this team cannot distinguish no gating from insufficient onset precision, from unrecoverable frontopolar ISF, from cross-device synchronisation error, from a filter returning phase on a signal with no oscillation, from a fallback predictor that tests something else. Every one of those produces the same null, and a funded three-year project with one publishable outcome and one uninterpretable one is a poor use of a grant. This is cheap to fix, and the controls are already recoverable from these exact recordings. First, reproduce the human sigma-to-heart-rate infraslow coupling within participant, from ZMax sigma against EmbracePlus PPG — Lecci et al. report it in humans with a clear time lag, and Carro-Domínguez et al. quantify it as heart rate significantly higher at the sigma peak with an ~18° offset. That single analysis simultaneously validates the frontal phase estimate, the cross-device alignment and the achievable phase resolution, which are the three things a null would otherwise be blamed on. Second, reproduce the phase distribution of spontaneous microarousals against the ISF and check it against Dimitriades et al. — an arousal outcome with no dependence on hot flashes at all. Third, state an equivalence bound: name the smallest phase modulation you would regard as mechanistically meaningful and pre-commit to reporting equivalence when the interval falls inside it, conditional on the controls passing. Then say explicitly that a null is interpretable only if the controls pass, and that if they fail the study reports as a feasibility study. Naming your own kill criterion would do more for this application with me than any of the rhetoric in the Summary.
    Because the cycle is short, the binding constraint is not event count but the precision with which onset can be timed against it. [DRAFT.md L79-80]
  • Moderate The load-bearing anchor for the whole timing chain is the wrist electrodermal inflection, and it is asserted with no citation. Recent concurrent-PSG work on the Wearanize+ dataset — the dataset the draft itself cites for synchronisation — reports that tonic wrist EDA during sleep shows an inverted stage pattern, highest in N3, attributed to sweat accumulation under the device during periods of reduced movement, and concludes it reflects skin hydration rather than sympathetic activity and should not be used as a sympathetic arousal proxy in sleep. Phasic EDA fared better but showed no relationship to micro-arousal frequency. That confound generates slow conductance rises with the same shape as a flash, and it is stage-dependent, therefore correlated with sigma power, therefore potentially correlated with the predictor. I accept the caveats — that work used the E4 rather than the EmbracePlus and concerned tonic level rather than change-point detection of a phasic rise — so this does not prove your method fails. It does shift the burden. Your only validity anchor for wrist EDA is a paper using a hard-wired laboratory sensor on three women in a temperature-controlled room. Cite this evidence and answer it: report the change-point detector's ability to discriminate flash rises from sweat-accumulation ramps, report the EmbracePlus EDA sampling rate, resolution and noise floor against the 2 µS/30 s criterion, and if the manufacturer does not publish them, measure them. The cleanest answer is to add a sternal skin-conductance channel on a subsample of EEG nights and define both detection and onset from it, with the wrist as adjunct.
    Onset is back-dated by change-point detection to the inflection at which the electrodermal rise begins, not to a threshold crossing. [DRAFT.md L259-261]
  • Moderate Bedroom temperature is absent from this document — no logging, no covariate, no mention in the risk section — and it is the best-established environmental modulator of nocturnal flashes. Freedman and Roehrs, cited twice here for the REM result, showed in the same paper that an 18 °C ambient temperature reduced flash count from 2.2 to 1.5, with the effect confined to the first half of the night. Ambient temperature also raises tonic skin conductance directly, so it moves the detector's own input and its false-positive rate, and it interacts with the wrist sweat-accumulation confound above. These are home recordings spread across seasons in Dutch bedrooms, with bedding, sleepwear, heating state and bed-sharing unrecorded. That is a large uncontrolled source of variance in both the supply of events and the probability of detecting them, and a bedside temperature and humidity logger costs almost nothing and imposes no participant burden. Enter mean and within-night bedroom temperature as covariates in both models with a temperature-by-half-of-night term, record the bedding and bed-sharing items in the morning diary, and name ambient temperature in the risk section as a modifier of flash rate and of detector specificity. While there: the half-of-night covariate is currently justified by a contested finding stated as fact. Your own cited review records that one study found awakenings more likely before than after a flash, another found flashes preceding awakenings only in the first half, and others found flashes and awakenings largely coincident with no first-versus-second-half difference — including De Zambotti et al., which you cite elsewhere for your headline prevalence figures. Keep the covariate, drop the certainty, and note that if arousal frequently precedes the flash the causal arrow in your supporting aim is reversed.
    the flash-arousal ordering reverses across the night: flashes precede arousals in the first half, arousals precede flashes in the second. [DRAFT.md L145-147]
  • Minor Two structural points a specialist will make immediately. First, the claim that this literature rests entirely on delivered stimuli is contradicted two sentences earlier by the draft's own text: 'in humans the fragility phase is associated with spontaneous arousals and transitions to lighter sleep' (L102-103). Spontaneous arousals are endogenous events already shown to be phase-structured, and Dimitriades et al. have now shown it in 154 people. So the novelty is narrower than claimed — an interoceptive, thermoregulatory event, and conscious report as the outcome — and stating it narrowly is stronger than stating it broadly and being corrected in the room. The related claim at L52-54 that quiet events are ones 'an experimenter-delivered stimulus can never provide' is simply false: sub-threshold tones producing neither arousal nor report are trivially deliverable and are standard in arousal-threshold work. The distinguishing property of the flash is endogeneity, not the existence of quiet events. Second, an entire adjacent literature is missing: the word CAP does not appear in this document. There is a published commentary on Lecci et al. arguing that the sigma infraslow oscillation may be a subharmonic of, or phase-locked to, the cyclic alternating pattern, and the CAP literature already contains the closest analogue of this proposal's hypothesis — periodic limb movements, endogenous and objectively timed, synchronising with CAP phase A. That is precedent support for your premise, not competition, and omitting it makes the proposal read as reinventing infraslow NREM microstructure without acknowledgement. You have roughly 1,100 characters of headroom in the Literature Review; two sentences on CAP would convert your largest citation gap into your strongest precedent.
    This literature rests entirely on stimuli delivered by an experimenter, a design that deliberately randomises stimulus timing against brain state. [DRAFT.md L115-117]
  • Minor A set of defects that individually are trivial and collectively tell me this was not read through. The sigma band is given as 11-16 Hz here and in the Summary and matches none of the cited sources: Lecci used 10-15 Hz, the Osorio-Forero file supplied with this application gives 10-15 Hz throughout, Dimitriades used 10-16 Hz, the device validation defines sigma as 13-16 Hz, and Lazar's infraslow oscillation was most prominent in the high sigma band, 13-15 Hz — the fast centro-parietal spindle population, which is not what a frontopolar montage samples. Four band definitions are in play, none is chosen, and the 16 Hz upper edge abuts the arousal criterion on the same derivations, inviting leakage between predictor and outcome. Lecci et al. (2017) is cited four times and is the empirical foundation of the entire rationale, and it is absent from the reference list; Osorio-Forero et al. (2025) is cited for a substantive result and appears only under previous publications; van Baarzel et al. is never cited at the point where the cohort is described, so a reader cannot identify the cohort at all. Osorio-Forero et al. (2021) appears twice in the reference list in two formats. The Wassing entry is prefixed with a markdown hash and will render as a section heading. There is a stray asterisk after the Rothhaas DOI. Escaped apostrophes survive at L34 and L119. The ethics reference is the literal string '[number]'. And in the single sentence that defines how the primary predictor is computed, the draft says 'the IAF phase' — IAF conventionally means individual alpha frequency, and I cannot tell from the document whether that is a typo or a misunderstanding of what is being filtered. In the methods section of a competitive application, that ambiguity is expensive. There is also no section named 'Specific Aims', which the regulation states is the section the objectives are assessed against, no Host Entity, no schedule and no budget in Euro.
    Lecci et al. (2017) described an oscillation of sigma-band (11-16 Hz) power at approximately 0.02 Hz [DRAFT.md L95-96] ... the Hilbert transform to calculate the IAF phase [DRAFT.md L269]
  • Minor The closing paragraph makes three claims it cannot support and ends the application on the sentence a hostile reviewer will read aloud. A phase effect on registration would not explain the report gap: the gap is a count over a whole night, a phase effect is a within-cycle probability, so at best it says some flashes are less likely to be noticed — which is the observation, not an explanation of it. The premise that treating flashes does not reliably resolve the sleep complaint is contradicted by the draft's own primary review, which states that the link between flashes and sleep disturbance 'is further supported by studies showing that the treatment of hot flashes with hormone therapy reduces sleep disturbances'. And structurally this is a therapeutic claim in a proposal to a funder that excludes clinical models of human disease and therapy, placed in the last paragraph, immediately after the sentence asserting the work is done 'without intervention', in an application whose cohort is an undisclosed therapy trial. The underlying intuition is defensible on evidence you do not cite — there is work showing menopause-associated NREM beta hyperarousal that survives statistical control for self-reported hot flashes, and mediation evidence that a majority of a neurokinin antagonist's sleep benefit is not mediated by flash reduction — but that is a different argument, and one of those sources is conference-presented rather than published. Cut the sentence, end on the mechanistic contribution, and let the clinical relevance stay implicit. Related: reframe the sample criterion physiologically — a minimum detected nocturnal event rate — rather than clinically ('flashes interfere with sleep'), and state early and explicitly that the study relates a mental event to concurrently recorded physical responses in healthy women during a normal reproductive transition, which is psychophysiology in the strict sense the regulation names and is the frame that should dominate this document.
    why women report far fewer nocturnal hot flashes than they have, and why treating the flashes does not reliably resolve the sleep complaint that accompanies them. [DRAFT.md L371-373]

What would change my mind

Pilot data, not promises, on the three things the study rests on — and I mean numbers from these women on these recordings, in the application. (1) Frontal ISF, demonstrated: per-participant infraslow spectral peak in the log sigma envelope from F7/F8-Fpz in at least ten of the cohort's existing nights, tested against interval-shuffled surrogates that preserve spindle count and individual refractoriness, and against a concurrent central derivation in a small simultaneous-PSG subsample, with the phase-error distribution between frontal and central reported. If the frontal envelope does not carry a peak that beats surrogates, no amount of statistical care rescues this design and the honest move is to add a central channel or a device that offers one. (2) Onset error, measured against a reference: one laboratory night per a handful of participants with simultaneous sternal skin conductance, reporting the bias and SD of the change-point back-dated onset against expert-scored gold standard, expressed as a fraction of each participant's own period rather than a nominal 50 s. Bias matters more than variance here and only a reference standard can see it: a systematic lag rotates the estimated preferred phase 7.2° per second, so without a bias bound under a few seconds the direction of your result is not interpretable, only its presence. (3) A causal phase estimator plus a negative control: phase estimated from a pre-onset window only, and the primary model recomputed with phase taken from a matched epoch one full cycle earlier, where a true gating effect must vanish. If the earlier-cycle control shows the same association, the finding is filter leakage from the outcome and we will both know it before any data are unblinded. Alongside those: invert the analysis hierarchy so cortical arousal among all detected flashes and registration among aroused flashes are the two pre-registered confirmatory tests, with a directionally agnostic prediction citing Dimitriades et al. (2026) and Carro-Domínguez et al. (2025) rather than a prediction of low-sigma fragility that the human literature contradicts; define stable NREM as ≥280 s pre-onset only, following the published human ISF studies, and meet low yield with more nights rather than a shorter window; supply the yield table and a real power curve with a named minimum effect of interest; put an operational definition on the button-press outcome; state that scoring is blinded and locked before the merge; and disclose the parent trial, name the timepoint, name the Host Entity, and give me a budget in Euro that makes clear Bial is funding the analysis and the added measurement rather than data collection NWO has already paid for. Do that and this becomes a proposal I would argue for in the room — the question is worth it, and nobody else is positioned to ask it.

Consciousness scientist — revise and resubmit, overall 7

Summary

This proposal has a genuinely good idea inside it: replace the experimenter's tone with an event the body generates on its own schedule, and ask whether an endogenous brain rhythm decides which of those events is noticed. That is a real advance in paradigm, and it is the kind of mind-body question Bial exists to fund — a mental event (noticing) set against concurrently recorded physical responses (sudomotor, vascular, cardiac) and brain state. I want to be persuaded by it. I am not, as written, for three reasons that sit squarely in my remit rather than in the statistics. First, the proposal claims to join "consciousness science" and never engages any theory of conscious access. It names no framework, derives no prediction from one, and specifies no result that would adjudicate between any two. Run the frameworks through it and each absorbs a positive result without learning anything: on a global-workspace account report requires ignition and NREM suppresses it, so a phase effect on a press is a phase effect on the transition to wake; on higher-order accounts a null on the press says nothing about first-order interoceptive representation; on recurrent-processing accounts most flashes are felt and never pressed, so press-versus-no-press indexes access and attention, not experience. The draft itself concedes the collapse — "Because a button press requires sufficient arousal, registered flashes are expected to be largely a subset of aroused ones" — and then designates that near-nested outcome as the confirmatory test while relegating the one analysis that could separate access from arousal to the exploratory tier. Second, the measure cannot bear the interpretation. A single binary press "made as soon as the participant thinks she is having a flash" is a conjunction of interoceptive signal, arousal sufficient for volitional action, correct causal attribution of a bodily state to a flash, motor execution and compliance, with no confidence rating, no catch trials, and no rule for presses with no matched flash — therefore no false-alarm estimate and no way to separate perceptual sensitivity from response criterion. In the one adjacent literature that has done this properly — cardiac and respiratory phase modulation of conscious tactile detection — the authors needed d-prime, criterion and meta-d-prime/d-prime to make the claim at all, and found effects of roughly four percentage points in 41 fully awake participants. This design cannot compute any of those quantities. A phase effect on presses is exactly as well explained by a phase-dependent willingness to wake up and act as by a phase-dependent gate on awareness, and the proposal has no instrument that tells the two apart. Third, a construct problem the proposal never sees. A hot flash is not an afferent signal arriving at a gate; it is a heat-dissipation effector response commanded by the hypothalamus, accompanied by a fourfold rise in skin sympathetic nerve activity. What the woman notices is the re-afferent consequence of her own brain's autonomic output. The proposal then hypothesises that the same infraslow noradrenergic system issues that command, sets the arousal threshold, and gates the percept. On its own mechanistic story, "the body reaching the mind" is the brain detecting its own echo — and a positive result is not distinguishable from the brain having shouted louder at itself. The draft half-registers this as an occurrence confound and states the right estimand in the literature review ("comparable events have different probabilities"), then abandons it in the analysis section by making the magnitude-unadjusted total effect confirmatory. Around these, the technical work has already found the failures that would break this on contact with data, and I endorse the important ones: a zero-phase filter estimates the predictor from EEG recorded after the outcome, which manufactures the predicted association; the ISF is centro-parietal and this device is frontopolar; the human evidence puts arousal markers at the sigma peak, so the pre-registered direction is probably inverted; the detector comes from three postmenopausal women on different hardware evaluated at plus-or-minus 90 seconds against a 50-second cycle; and there is no power analysis, no budget, no schedule, no Host Entity, and no section called Specific Aims. The cohort is an undisclosed four-arm hormone-therapy and CBT-I trial in women with clinical insomnia, which engages Bial's therapy exclusion and makes "physically healthy and take no hormone-altering medication" and "without intervention" untrue as written. The mechanistic section is the weakest kind of padding — mechanism-shopping. The KNDy-to-median-preoptic noradrenergic step is not in the source cited for it, all five major neuromodulators oscillate synchronously at 0.02 Hz so nothing selects noradrenaline, and the sign of the noradrenaline-sigma relation is misread. None of it is needed. The question stands or falls on the psychophysics, and I would rather read a page of psychophysics than a page of mouse locus coeruleus. Revise and resubmit. The paradigm is worth funding; this instrumentation of it is not.

Objections raised

  • Major The proposal claims membership of consciousness science and tests no theory of conscious access. No framework is named, no prediction is derived from one, and no result is specified that would discriminate between any two accounts. I applied the obvious candidates myself: on a global-workspace account, report during sleep requires the very long-range ignition that NREM suppresses, so a phase effect on a press is a phase effect on the transition toward wake; on higher-order accounts a null is uninformative about first-order interoceptive representation and a graded confidence measure would be mandatory; on recurrent-processing accounts local recurrence suffices for experience without report, so the press-versus-no-press contrast tracks access and attention rather than the arrival of the body in the mind; integrated-information accounts would look at post-onset cortical dynamics and not at a motor act. Each framework reinterprets a positive result as arousal-threshold modulation. I am left unable to say what this project would teach anyone about consciousness, as opposed to about arousability, and that is the criterion I am here to guard.
    It brings together sleep neuroscience, neuroendocrinology and consciousness science around a question about the sleeping human: when does the body reach the mind during sleep?
  • Major The primary outcome cannot separate awareness from response threshold, and the design forecloses the only methods that could. A single binary press aggregates at least five things — interoceptive signal reaching cortex, arousal sufficient for volitional action, correct causal attribution of the bodily state to a flash, motor execution, and compliance — and the draft's own wording concedes the attribution step by making the criterion what the participant thinks. There is no confidence rating, no catch trials, and no rule for presses with no matched detected flash, so no false-alarm rate can be estimated and neither sensitivity nor criterion is identifiable. The closest properly conducted precedent — cardiac and respiratory phase modulation of conscious tactile detection (Grund et al., J Neurosci 2022, n=41) — required d-prime, response criterion and meta-d-prime/d-prime to license its claim, reported detection differences of roughly 3.8 percentage points and R = 0.34, and explicitly checked that greater detection reflected sensitivity rather than a more liberal criterion. This design can compute none of that. A phase effect on presses is equally well explained by phase-dependent willingness to wake and act, which is arousability again.
    Conscious registration is indexed by a time-stamped button press made as soon as the participant thinks she is having a flash; morning reports give a complementary measure of recall and compliance.
  • Major The proposal designates as confirmatory the one analysis that cannot demonstrate its central claim, and designates as exploratory the one that could. Decompose it: P(registered | phase) = P(aroused | phase) x P(registered | aroused, phase). Phase-dependent arousability is what Lecci et al. already established. Only the second factor isolates access over and above arousal, and the draft itself says registered flashes are largely a subset of aroused ones — then makes the total registration model confirmatory and the arousal-conditioned model exploratory. A significant primary result is therefore produced by pure arousal gating with no gating of access whatever, and the proposal's headline interpretation would not follow from its own confirmatory test. Worse, the draft forbids conditioning on magnitude on mediator grounds two paragraphs later while freely conditioning on arousal, which is equally a post-onset mediator. The inferential hierarchy is inverted.
    Because a button press requires sufficient arousal, registered flashes are expected to be largely a subset of aroused ones; the joint distribution is reported and registration additionally modelled among aroused flashes.
  • Major The predictor is estimated from data recorded after the outcome. A zero-phase band-pass at 0.01-0.04 Hz is non-causal by construction, with an impulse response spanning tens of seconds on both sides of every sample, so the phase assigned to a flash onset depends on sigma-band power after that onset. Both outcomes — a cortical arousal and a press requiring wakefulness — systematically change post-onset sigma and add movement artefact, and the draft's own account of fragility is spindle loss and arousal. The filter propagates that post-onset drop backwards into the estimated onset phase, pulling registered and aroused flashes toward fragility with zero true gating. Against a 50-second cycle a few seconds of leakage is tens of degrees. The circularity discussion in this draft is entirely about the flash detector and never touches this, which is the far larger circularity. This alone would invalidate a positive confirmatory result.
    Instantaneous ISF phase is obtained from the log sigma envelope by zero-phase band-pass filtering (0.01-0.04 Hz, empirical peak reported per participant) and the Hilbert transform to calculate the IAF phase.
  • Major The object of study is not an interoceptive signal arriving at a gate; it is the re-afferent consequence of the brain's own autonomic command, and the proposal's own mechanism makes that fatal to the framing. A hot flash is a heat-dissipation effector response accompanied by a fourfold rise in skin sympathetic nerve activity (Gombert-Labedens et al., 2025, the draft's own source). The proposal then hypothesises that one infraslow noradrenergic rhythm issues that command, sets the arousal threshold, and gates the percept. On that story, a phase effect on registration is indistinguishable from the brain having generated a louder peripheral event at that phase and then having been less able to sleep through its own output. The title question presupposes an afferent signal and an independent gate; the mechanism supplies neither. This is a construct-validity problem, not a covariate problem, and adjusting for magnitude does not fix it — which is why the draft's decision to make the magnitude-unadjusted total effect confirmatory abandons the correct estimand its own literature review had stated.
    That nucleus is also where autonomic thermoregulation and sleep-wake control converge, and it receives noradrenergic input, raising the possibility that a single infraslow rhythm times arousability and thermoeffector drive together (Rothhaas & Chung, 2021).
  • Major The proposal cites the one paper that hands it a no-report interoceptive measure and then does not use it. Cataldi et al. (2026) is a 25-participant high-density EEG study of auditory versus heartbeat evoked potentials in which no subjective report was collected at all, and whose authors propose their audio-cardio index precisely as a marker "particularly informative in contexts where behavioral responsiveness cannot be assessed". Sleep is the paradigm case of such a context. The draft cites this for a dissociation claim and then builds its entire primary outcome on volitional behavioural responsiveness. A flash-locked evoked response, and a flash-locked change in the heartbeat-evoked potential, would give a measure of the signal reaching cortex that does not require waking, converting the design from one rung (report) into three (cortical response, arousal, report) — which is the only version of this study that can honestly claim to be about interoceptive access rather than arousal threshold. The relevant group is in Lausanne, as is the rodent collaborator already claimed on the team.
    Cataldi et al. (2026) compared auditory and heartbeat evoked potentials across wakefulness and REM microstates and found a dissociation, with auditory responses declining progressively into phasic REM while cardiac responses were preserved and enhanced.
  • Major The pre-registered direction is probably inverted, and it is inverted against the applicants' own collaborator's human data. Lecci et al. define the arousal-prone phase by the derivative of sigma power — wake-ups during declining, sleep-throughs during rising — not by its level; Osorio-Forero et al. targeted arousability by rising versus declining sigma and report noradrenaline peaking before sigma declines. In humans, the largest characterisation of the infraslow sigma fluctuation to date (Dimitriades, Osorio-Forero, Fattinger et al., Sci Rep 2026, n=154) places microarousals around the spindle-rich peak, and Carro-Domínguez et al. (Nat Commun 2025) report human heart rate highest at the sigma peak, explicitly opposite to mice. So the draft's equation of fragility with low sigma power is a misreading of its own team's work, and the human literature points the other way. The sin/cos test survives; the prose commitment in Expected Outcomes does not, and a reviewer who knows the 2026 paper — whose second author the applicants invoke as their expertise claim — will read this as evidence the human literature on the predictor has not been read.
    Extending the exogenous literature, flashes arriving in fragility (low sigma power) are predicted to be more likely registered, and followed by an arousal, than those in continuity.
  • Major The contingency plan silently substitutes a different hypothesis for the one under test. The primary question is about when within a cycle an event arrives — a claim about temporal alignment, and the whole reason the design is interesting, because phase is orthogonal to mean sleep depth within a bout. Pre-flash amplitude is a state-level quantity, ambiguous between modulation depth and instantaneous sigma level, confounded with N2 versus N3, spindle density and time of night, and symmetric across the rising and falling limbs that the source literature says carry opposite arousability. Its tolerance to timing error is not a virtue; it is the symptom of having discarded the temporal information the hypothesis is about. And the second trigger is self-defeating: if frontal ISF expression is too weak to give reliable phase, it is too weak to give meaningful amplitude, since both are read off the same envelope. Presenting this as robustness rather than as abandonment is the single sentence in the draft I would read aloud in the panel.
    the primary predictor switches from ISF phase to pre-flash ISF amplitude, which tolerates far more timing error while testing the same hypothesis; weak frontal ISF expression triggers the same rule.
  • Moderate The founding observation of the proposal is the applicants' own inference presented as a citation, and it begs the question the study asks. The cited review contains nothing about whether nocturnal flashes are consciously registered at the time they occur. What it reports is that roughly 20 to 29 per cent of objectively detected flashes occur without disturbing sleep — an EEG-defined absence of arousal — and that flashes during sleep may be under-reported retrospectively in the morning, which is an absence of recall. Neither is a statement about awareness. Conflating undisturbed sleep with unregistered experience, and morning under-report with never having been noticed, is precisely the inferential step this project exists to test. A reviewer who opens the reference finds the premise unsupported by the source given for it, and the same conflation of measurement, derived evidence and interpretation runs through the whole draft.
    Interestingly enough, just as with external signals, they are sometimes consciously registered, and other times leave no trace (Gombert-Labedens et al., 2025).
  • Moderate Mechanism-shopping, and the shopping list does not check out. The convergence argument turns on noradrenergic input to the median preoptic nucleus, and the cited review presents its noradrenergic evidence for the ventrolateral preoptic area and for projection-defined populations, not the MnPO, and contains no mention of KNDy neurons, oestrogen, menopause or hot flashes at all. Meanwhile all five major neuromodulators — acetylcholine, serotonin, dopamine, histamine and noradrenaline — oscillate synchronously at about 0.02 Hz in NREM with no difference in peak frequency (Kjaerby et al., iScience 2025), so nothing in the argument selects noradrenaline; and the sign runs the wrong way, since noradrenaline inhibits preoptic sleep-active neurons. This apparatus is not load-bearing for the psychological question and it is partly wrong. Strip it, state the shared-rhythm idea as a conjecture the study does not test, and spend the recovered characters on psychophysics. The strongest genuine link — that an alpha-2 antagonist provokes flashes and an agonist suppresses them — sits unused on a page of the review the draft already cites.
    In rodents this fluctuation tracks locus coeruleus (LC) activity.
  • Major The primary outcome has no operational definition anywhere in the document. Nothing states the window within which a press counts as registering a given flash — a flash lasts one to five minutes, and waking, orienting and locating a wristband button takes a time that will itself vary with depth of sleep, which is the predictor, and that plausibly exceeds a whole ISF cycle. Nothing states what happens when one press falls near two flashes, when several presses fall near one, when a press has no detected flash at all, or when a press occurs during scored wake while the analysis is restricted to stable NREM. Different defensible windows produce different outcome vectors and therefore different confirmatory results from identical data, and the unmatched presses that are simply unaddressed are exactly the observations that would have given a false-alarm rate. This must be fully pre-specified with sensitivity analyses at stated alternatives before the pre-registration means anything.
    On EEG nights participants press a wristband button as soon as they think they are having a flash; this time-stamped press is a prospective measure of conscious registration.
  • Major The one quantitative statement in the power section is mathematically false, and it is what licenses the proposal to state no event count at all. Independent onset jitter attenuates a circular effect multiplicatively — by exp(-(2*pi*sigma/T)^2/2) — inflating the required N by the reciprocal of that factor squared. It does not impose a ceiling: power is strictly increasing in N at every jitter level. So the claim that additional events stop helping is the opposite of what the model does, and the framing that precision rather than event count binds is contradicted by the draft's own justification for four nights. Consequently there is no expected number of analysable flashes, no expected number of registered events, no target effect size, no minimum detectable effect, and "simulation shows" is written in the past tense for a simulation the next sentence says depends on data that do not exist. Given that the adjacent awake literature finds effects of a few percentage points, the plausible effect here is small, and I cannot distinguish a design with eighty informative events from one with eight hundred.
    The binding constraint is measurement precision rather than event count: onset jitter translates directly into phase uncertainty against a 50-s cycle, and simulation shows power ceasing to improve with additional events once jitter exceeds a quarter of the cycle.
  • Major The predictor may not be measurable with this device, and the two citations offered as feasibility support both report the opposite. Lazar et al. (2019) find the infraslow sigma oscillation most prominent centro-parieto-occipitally and report frontopolar electrodes as having the lowest infraslow power of any region; Lecci et al.'s human recordings are C3 and C4. The ZMax provides only F7-Fpz and F8-Fpz. A small bias in mean relative sigma bandpower is a static offset that the band-pass removes entirely and says nothing about the fidelity of the sigma envelope at 0.02 Hz, which is the only quantity that matters here. The draft concedes the gap two sentences later by calling frontal expression a feasibility outcome, while still asserting that feasibility is supported. This should be a hard pre-registered gate with a central derivation available as the remedy, not a citation pointed in the wrong direction.
    Feasibility is supported: sigma-band power from this headband shows the smallest bias of any band against polysomnography (0.005 ± 0.012; Esfahani et al., 2023), and the infraslow modulation of sigma is established in humans (Lecci et al., 2017; Lazar et al., 2019).
  • Major The eligibility statement is untrue and the host study is undisclosed. The 222-woman cohort is the applicants' own four-arm randomised trial of transdermal estradiol plus progesterone and online cognitive behavioural and circadian therapy for insomnia, enrolling women with an Insomnia Severity Index of 10 or higher, with the device package collected at three timepoints including two on treatment. Hormone therapy suppresses vasomotor symptoms by roughly 75 per cent and therapy for insomnia alters arousal thresholds and spindle expression, so half the arms perturb the outcome and a quarter perturb the predictor. The draft never states which timepoint supplies the nights, describes participants as physically healthy on hormone-altering-medication-free terms that hold only at entry, and asserts elsewhere that the work is done without intervention. This engages the exclusion of projects involving clinical models of human disease and therapy, and non-disclosure converts a scope question a reviewer might have decided generously into a candour question. Disclose the trial, restrict to the pre-randomisation block, and argue the scope point explicitly rather than by adjective.
    They are physically healthy and take no hormone-altering medication; other medication is documented, with attention to agents suppressing vasomotor symptoms.
  • Moderate The proposal ends on a therapeutic claim that is uncited, contradicted by its own source, and addressed to a funder that excludes therapy. The review the draft leans on for flash physiology states the opposite — that hormone therapy for hot flashes reduces sleep disturbance, and that neurokinin-antagonist trials improved sleep quality and reduced awakenings. Better evidence for the underlying idea exists and is not cited. More importantly, this is the last thing a Scientific Board member reads, and it converts a psychophysiological proposal into a clinical one in a single sentence. Cut it and end on the mechanistic contribution.
    It would also give a mechanistic account of a clinical puzzle - why women report far fewer nocturnal hot flashes than they have, and why treating the flashes does not reliably resolve the sleep complaint that accompanies them.
  • Moderate The novelty claim is over-stated in two directions, and the corrections would strengthen rather than weaken the case. Two sentences earlier the draft cites human evidence involving no delivered stimulus at all — spontaneous arousals and spindle-poor substates are endogenous events already shown to be phase-structured — and an entire prior literature on infraslow NREM microstructure gating endogenous events is absent: the cyclic alternating pattern, a published commentary arguing that the sigma oscillation may be synchronised with it, and periodic limb movements clustering in CAP phase A.
