That literature is the closest existing precedent for this proposal's own premise, and citing it converts the largest gap in the review into the strongest support. Equally, phase of a bodily rhythm already predicts conscious detection in wakefulness, which is the intellectual lineage of this project and is uncited. And the claim that quiet events are something a delivered stimulus can never provide is simply false — sub-threshold tones producing neither arousal nor report are standard. The distinguishing property is endogeneity, not quietness.
    This literature rests entirely on stimuli delivered by an experimenter, a design that deliberately randomises stimulus timing against brain state.
  • Moderate There is no positive control, so a null is uninterpretable and a three-year project has one publishable outcome. A null would be equally consistent with no gating, insufficient onset precision, frontopolar ISF too weak to estimate, cross-device synchronisation error, and the fallback predictor testing the wrong construct. Two controls are already available in these exact recordings and cost nothing: reproduce the human sigma-to-heart-rate infraslow coupling within participant from headband sigma against wristband PPG, which validates the phase estimate, the synchronisation and the achievable resolution in one step; and reproduce the phase distribution of spontaneous microarousals against the ISF, which validates the predictor against an arousal outcome with no dependence on hot flashes at all. Without these, and without a pre-registered equivalence bound, the study cannot report a negative result and should not be described as confirmatory.
    Because the cycle is short, the binding constraint is not event count but the precision with which onset can be timed against it.
  • Moderate Form compliance, which I mention last because it is the easiest to fix and the quickest route to rejection by someone who never reaches the science. There is no Host Entity or Research Centre designated, which the regulation makes a condition of eligibility; no budget in euro against a 60,000 euro ceiling with overheads and equipment-use costs non-reimbursable and the data collection already funded by NWO; no schedule and no start date inside the 1 January to 31 October 2027 window; no CVs; and no section headed Specific Aims, which is the section the regulation states the application is assessed against and the final report checked against. The ethics reference is a literal placeholder in a sentence asserting completed approval, and the approval that exists covers the host trial and not the nocturnal button press, the tap markers or the morning flash diary, none of which appear in that protocol. Separately, the most heavily cited work in the proposal — Lecci et al. 2017, cited four times and carrying the entire premise — is absent from the reference list, one reference is duplicated, one renders as a section heading, and the sentence defining the primary predictor calls it the IAF phase.
    The study is approved by the Medical Ethics Review Committee of Amsterdam UMC (reference [number]).

What would change my mind

Four changes, in priority order, and I would then advocate for this. 1. Add a no-report outcome to the same events. Time-lock an evoked response to the electrodermal change point, and measure a flash-locked change in the heartbeat-evoked potential, following the draft's own cited Cataldi et al. (2026) — whose authors propose exactly this class of index for contexts where behavioural responsiveness cannot be assessed. That converts a one-rung design into three rungs (cortical response to the interoceptive event, arousal, report), gives a measure of the signal reaching cortex that does not require waking, and is the only version of this project that can address interoceptive access rather than arousal threshold. The relevant expertise is in Lausanne, where the claimed rodent collaborator already sits. 2. Make the report measure criterion-controlled. Add a confidence rating to each press, define the matching window and the treatment of unmatched presses so a false-alarm rate exists, and pre-specify a sensitivity-versus-criterion analysis. Without a false-alarm estimate there is no d-prime, no criterion, and therefore no defensible claim that phase moved awareness rather than the threshold for acting. The wakefulness literature on cardiac-phase gating of conscious detection did this and found effects of a few percentage points; anchor the power simulation to that magnitude. 3. Invert the confirmatory hierarchy and estimate the predictor causally. Pre-register two confirmatory tests: phase to cortical arousal among all detected flashes (the replication, and the informative one), and phase to registration among aroused flashes or as a natural direct effect in a mediation model with arousal as mediator (the quantity that isolates access). Estimate ISF phase from pre-onset data only with a causal estimator, and demonstrate on an outcome-shuffled surrogate and on a phase estimate taken one full cycle earlier that no association survives. As it stands the confirmatory test is a replication of phase-dependent arousability, and the predictor is contaminated by the outcome. 4. Say what theory this adjudicates, in three sentences, and name a result that would embarrass one account and favour another. Then delete the KNDy and locus coeruleus apparatus, which is decorative, partly unsupported by the sources cited for it, and does not select noradrenaline over the four other neuromodulators oscillating at the same frequency. Also fix the direction: state the phases by the derivative of sigma as the source work does, cite the human evidence placing arousal markers at the peak, and let the sin/cos test remain two-sided. Alongside these: disclose the host randomised trial, restrict to the pre-randomisation block, add a Host Entity, a euro budget, a schedule, CVs, a Specific Aims section, the real ethics reference with the amendment status of the button press, and the missing Lecci reference. Add the two zero-cost positive controls so that a null is interpretable. If the onset-precision gate cannot be closed with existing evidence, submit this as a feasibility and effect-estimation study with a stated kill criterion — I would score that far more generously than a confirmatory framing the applicants themselves cannot yet support.

Methodologist / statistician — revise and resubmit, overall 7

Summary

A genuinely good question wrapped around a confirmatory design that cannot answer it in either direction. The proposal asks whether the phase of the ~0.02 Hz infraslow sigma fluctuation at nocturnal hot flash onset predicts whether the flash is consciously registered. That is novel, mechanistically motivated, and squarely psychophysiological. But the statistical core is absent and the identification is broken. Three things sink it as written. First, there is no expected number of analysable events anywhere in the document. The exclusion cascade is named at L204-206 and never computed; no event count, no effect size, no power figure, no minimum detectable effect appears. I built the yield chain myself from the draft's own numbers (137 women x 4 nights x ~0.6 usable EEG nights x 3.5 flashes/night x 0.75 not-already-awake x 0.85 NREM x ~0.5 stable-bout x 0.8 artefact/onset) and get roughly 300 analysable flashes, of which 45-125 registered. My own calculation of the 2-df sin/cos likelihood-ratio test gives, for an odds ratio of 2 between best and worst phase, a requirement of 1,258 events at zero jitter and 1,867 at 5 s onset jitter (press rate 0.15), or 654 and 971 at the draft's implied 43% report rate. The minimum detectable effect at N=300 with 5 s jitter is an odds ratio of 3.5 to 5.6. That is an implausibly large phase-gating effect: the closest published benchmark, cardiac and respiratory phase modulation of conscious tactile detection in wakefulness, is circular R around 0.34. The design is short by a factor of three to nine for any effect size a reviewer would find credible. Second, the one quantitative power claim in the document is mathematically false, and it is precisely the claim that licenses stating no N. Independent onset jitter of SD s against period T attenuates the first circular harmonic by exp(-(2*pi*s/T)^2/2); it shrinks the effect but leaves the estimator consistent, so power is strictly increasing in N at every finite jitter and there is no threshold past which events stop helping. I computed the inflation factors: 1.48x at 5 s, 4.04x at 9.4 s, 11.79x at the draft's own quarter-cycle (12.5 s), 34.9x at 15 s. Jitter does not bound power; it multiplies the required event count. Removing the false ceiling removes the argument for not stating N — and both constraints then bind simultaneously, contradicting the draft's own L191-192. Third, and worst, the predictor is estimated with a zero-phase filter. A non-causal band-pass at 0.01-0.04 Hz has an impulse response spanning tens of seconds in both directions, so the phase assigned to a flash onset depends on EEG recorded after that onset. Both outcomes — a cortical arousal and a button press requiring wakefulness — produce post-onset spindle suppression and movement artefact, i.e. a sigma drop, which the filter propagates backwards into the estimated onset phase and pulls it toward the "fragility" pole. The design therefore manufactures the predicted association with no gating whatever, and it manufactures it in exactly the direction the Expected Outcomes section pre-commits to. Combined with the sigma upper edge (16 Hz) abutting the arousal-defining band (>16 Hz) on the same two frontal derivations, this is a validity failure that makes a positive result as uninterpretable as a null. Layered on top: the designated confirmatory test is the least informative analysis in the proposal. Registration is largely a subset of arousal, as the draft itself states at L299-302. I verified the consequence: logit-scale amplitude transmits from the arousal model to the registration model with a factor of 0.353, and after the base-rate difference the registration test carries 7.6% of the non-centrality of the arousal test — it needs 13.2x the events. So the proposal nominates its weakest test as confirmatory, while the only analysis that isolates the advertised claim (registration among aroused flashes) is declared exploratory at L310-311 and conditions on a mediator the draft forbids adjusting for two paragraphs earlier at L306-309. There is no stated estimand, test statistic, or decision rule for the comparison the Summary promises at L54-56. Then the escape hatches. I count eleven named-but-empty decision thresholds, plus a twelfth that is worse: the primary outcome variable has no operational definition at all — no window within which a button press counts as registering a given flash, no rule for unmatched presses, multiply-matched presses, or presses during scored wake, against a flash lasting one to five minutes and a cycle of fifty seconds. Defensible choices of that one window produce materially different confirmatory results from the same data. And the pre-registered fallback (L341-343) substitutes pre-flash ISF amplitude while asserting it tests "the same hypothesis". It does not: amplitude is symmetric across the rising and falling limbs, which is the distinction the mechanism is about, and it is read off the same frontal envelope whose weakness triggers the switch. That sentence converts a null into something reportable as a positive. Finally, a null here would be uninterpretable, which is the design property I am least willing to fund. There is no positive control. A null is equally consistent with no gating, insufficient onset precision, unmeasurable frontal ISF, cross-device synchronisation error, and detector false positives — and the proposal acknowledges at L275-276 that two of those are unresolved. Two cheap controls are available in these exact recordings (recovering the human sigma-to-heart-rate infraslow coupling from ZMax sigma against EmbracePlus PPG; recovering the phase distribution of spontaneous microarousals) and neither is proposed. The feasibility gap at the binding constraint is unbridged: the draft sets its own tolerance at a quarter cycle (~12.5 s, and only ~6.25 s for a participant at the fast end of its own 0.01-0.04 Hz band) while the cited detector decides every 15 s and was scored against a ±90 s matching tolerance in three postmenopausal women on a bench-wired sensor array that is not the study device. The rhythm itself is reported centro-parietally maximal and frontopolar-minimal by both papers cited as feasibility support. And the cohort is not a cohort: 222 is the parent trial's enrolment target, 65 have been screened, and that parent trial is an undisclosed four-arm randomisation to estradiol/progesterone and CBT-I in women with ISI>=10 — so the timepoint supplying the nights determines both the yield (by a factor of three) and whether half the sample is on a drug that suppresses the outcome event by about 75%. The draft never states which timepoint it uses. The science is worth doing. The application is not fundable in this form, and the required changes are not editorial.

Objections raised

  • Major (L318-320.) There is no power analysis. This sentence describes a calculation in the future tense and the document never performs it: no expected number of analysable flashes, no expected number of registered events, no assumed effect size, no minimum detectable effect, no target power. I am being asked to fund a confirmatory test whose detectability is unstated. Worse, the preceding sentence reports a simulation in the present indicative ('simulation shows') that this sentence says cannot yet have been run. I did the arithmetic the applicants declined to do, using only their own figures: 137 women x 4 nights x ~0.6 usable EEG nights x 3.5 flashes x 0.75 asleep at onset x 0.85 NREM x ~0.5 stable-bout x 0.8 artefact-and-onset gives roughly 300 analysable flashes and 45-125 registered ones. For an odds ratio of 2 between best and worst phase, the joint sin/cos test needs 1,258 events at zero jitter and 1,867 at 5 s onset jitter (15% press rate), or 654 and 971 at the draft's implied 43% report rate. The minimum detectable effect at N=300 with 5 s jitter is an odds ratio of 3.5 to 5.6. The published benchmark for phase gating of conscious detection in wakefulness is circular R around 0.34 — far smaller. This design is short by a factor of three to nine for any credible effect, and the applicants cannot tell me otherwise because they never counted.
    Simulations use the observed counts and precision, and the minimum detectable effect is reported.
  • Major (L315-318.) This is the single most consequential error in the proposal, and it is not a hedge — it is arithmetically the opposite of what the model does. Independent onset jitter of SD s against a period T attenuates the first circular harmonic by exp(-(2*pi*s/T)^2/2). It shrinks the effect size; it does not add a variance floor. The estimator stays consistent, so power is strictly increasing in N at every finite jitter level and approaches 1. There is no threshold past which additional events stop helping. I computed the required-N inflation factors: 1.07x at 2 s, 1.48x at 5 s, 4.04x at 9.4 s, 11.79x at the quarter-cycle the sentence names, 34.9x at 15 s. Jitter multiplies the event requirement; it never caps it. I dwell on this because the false ceiling is load-bearing: it is exactly what licenses the claim that event count is not the binding constraint, and therefore what licenses stating no event count at all. Delete the ceiling and the proposal owes me a number it does not have. It also puts this sentence in direct contradiction with the Study design section at L191-192, which justifies four nights on the ground that power depends on event count. Both constraints bind, and they bind multiplicatively.
    The binding constraint is measurement precision rather than event count: onset jitter translates directly into phase uncertainty against a 50-s cycle, and simulation shows power ceasing to improve with additional events once jitter exceeds a quarter of the cycle.
  • Major (L267-269.) A zero-phase filter is non-causal. A band-pass whose low edge is 0.01 Hz has an effective impulse response of tens of seconds, applied forward and backward, so the instantaneous phase assigned to a flash onset is partly determined by EEG recorded after that onset. Now consider what the outcomes are. A cortical arousal is, on the draft's own account, marked by spindle suppression and a sigma drop; a button press requires the participant to wake enough to act, generating both an arousal and a large movement artefact within seconds of onset. So registered and aroused flashes systematically have post-onset sigma trajectories that differ from unregistered ones, and the non-causal filter propagates that difference backwards into the estimated pre-onset phase, pulling it toward the low-sigma pole. The design manufactures a phase-registration association with zero true gating — and it manufactures it in precisely the direction the Expected Outcomes section pre-commits to at L355-357. Against a 50 s cycle, a few seconds of leakage is tens of degrees. This is compounded by band adjacency: the predictor is 11-16 Hz sigma power and the arousal outcome is scored as >16 Hz activity, on the same two frontal derivations, so spectral leakage from the arousal itself is a second route to the same artefact. The proposal's entire circularity discussion at L246-254 concerns the flash detector and never touches this, which is by far the larger circularity. As it stands, a positive result is as uninterpretable as a null.
    Instantaneous ISF phase is obtained from the log sigma envelope by zero-phase band-pass filtering (0.01-0.04 Hz, empirical peak reported per participant) and the Hilbert transform to calculate the IAF phase.
  • Major (L310-311.) The proposal nominates its least informative analysis as the confirmatory one, and declares the only analysis that could demonstrate its central claim to be exploratory. Decompose: P(registered|phase) = P(aroused|phase) x P(registered|aroused, phase). The advertised novelty is that phase gates access to reportable awareness over and above arousability — but phase-dependent arousability is what Lecci et al. already established. If the first factor carries the effect, the confirmatory result is a replication using a spontaneous rather than a delivered stimulus. Only the second factor isolates the claim, and it is the demoted one. I verified the information cost of this choice: because registration is largely a subset of arousal (the draft says so at L299-302), logit-scale amplitude transmits from the arousal model to the registration model with a factor of 0.353, and after the base-rate difference the registration test carries 7.6% of the non-centrality of the arousal test — it requires 13.2 times the events. So the designated confirmatory test is thirteen times harder than the test called 'supporting', while being strictly less diagnostic of the hypothesis. And the demoted analysis conditions on arousal, a post-onset variable on the causal path from phase to registration — exactly the adjustment the draft forbids on principled mediator grounds two paragraphs earlier for magnitude. The proposal is internally incoherent about its own estimand. Finally, the Summary promises at L54-56 that 'comparing the two' distinguishes cortical gating from gating of access, and names no estimand, no test statistic and no decision rule for that comparison. Informally eyeballing two sin/cos coefficient pairs fitted to nested outcomes is not a test.
    The primary registration model is confirmatory; all else is exploratory.
  • Major (L340-343.) A pre-registration whose decision thresholds are described but not stated is not a pre-registration; it is a licence for post hoc latitude with the word 'pre-registered' attached. I counted eleven named-but-empty parameters: the threshold for dispersion of inter-marker intervals (L340); the criterion for 'weak frontal ISF expression' (L343); the event count that triggers 'low event yield' (L344); the compliance 'floor' below which participants are dropped (L347-348); the artefact criterion (L206); the onset-reliability criterion (L206); the definition of 'stable' NREM, which appears only obliquely forty lines later as three ISF cycles (L270, L344-345); the rule if no empirical ISF peak is identifiable (L268); the minimum detectable effect (L319-320); the maximum acceptable device-synchronisation residual (L229-230); and the 'estimation window' listed as an exclusion and never defined (L206). Bial assesses the project against the objectives as submitted and checks the final report against them. Objectives whose decision rules are blank can be neither assessed nor verified. Put a number on each. A stated kill criterion strengthens an application; eleven blanks weaken it.
    if it exceeds a pre-registered threshold, the primary predictor switches from ISF phase to pre-flash ISF amplitude, which tolerates far more timing error while testing the same hypothesis; weak frontal ISF expression triggers the same rule.
  • Major (L341-343.) This is the sentence I would read aloud in the panel. It is not the same hypothesis, and the claim that it is would let a null phase result be published as a positive finding about gating. The hypothesis is that WHEN within the cycle an event arrives determines whether it reaches awareness — a claim about temporal alignment, which is interesting precisely because phase is orthogonal to mean sleep depth within a bout. Pre-flash amplitude is a state-level scalar with no timing content. It is also symmetric across the rising and falling limbs of the cycle, and the rising-versus-falling distinction is exactly what the mechanism is about: Osorio-Forero et al. manipulated arousability by targeting whether sigma was rising or declining, and noradrenaline is high on the falling limb and low on the rising limb at matched sigma levels. An amplitude predictor averages over the two states the hypothesis concerns, so a null on amplitude is compatible with a strong phase effect and a positive on amplitude is compatible with none. It is additionally ambiguous between two constructs the draft never distinguishes — modulation depth of the rhythm versus instantaneous sigma level — both heavily confounded with N2/N3, spindle density and time of night, which is the confound the phase design exists to escape. And the second trigger is self-defeating: if frontal ISF expression is too weak to give reliable phase, it is too weak to give meaningful amplitude, because both are read off the same frontal envelope. The fallback inherits the failure it is invoked to escape. A phase-preserving, jitter-tolerant fallback exists — the binary sign of the sigma derivative at onset, which is the variable the team's own rodent work actually manipulated — and it is not proposed.
    the primary predictor switches from ISF phase to pre-flash ISF amplitude, which tolerates far more timing error while testing the same hypothesis
  • Major (L216-217.) The primary outcome variable has no operational definition. The confirmatory model predicts 'whether a detected flash is consciously registered' and the proposal never states what makes a detected flash registered. Missing: the time window after estimated onset within which a press counts — and a flash lasts one to five minutes, while a woman may wake, orient, locate a wristband button and press minutes later, or only at a subsequent awakening; the rule when one press falls near two detected flashes or several presses near one; the treatment of presses with no detected flash, which are direct evidence about detector sensitivity and reporting behaviour and are simply unaddressed; whether presses during scored wake count, given that analyses are restricted to stable NREM and a press necessarily follows an arousal, so the press timestamp will usually fall outside the very bout that supplied the phase estimate; and accidental presses in sleep. Different defensible windows — 30 s, 2 min, 5 min, next awakening — produce materially different outcome vectors and therefore different confirmatory results from identical data. That is unconstrained analytic freedom sitting on the primary endpoint of a study that calls itself pre-registered. Note also that press latency is expected to correlate with sleep depth, which is the predictor, so the window choice is not even neutral with respect to the hypothesis. The supporting outcome has the same defect: no interval within which an arousal counts as flash-related.
    On EEG nights participants press a wristband button as soon as they think they are having a flash; this time-stamped press is a prospective measure of conscious registration.
  • Major (L258-259, with L242-245 and L315-318.) The proposal names onset precision as the binding constraint and then inherits its onset timing from a pipeline that operates two orders of magnitude away from the requirement. A quarter of a 50 s cycle is 12.5 s. The cited detector makes one decision every 15 s, computes features over windows of ±30 s, ±120 s, ±250 s and ±500 s, and was scored against expert annotations using a ±90 s matching window — a tolerance of nearly four ISF cycles, i.e. ±648 degrees of phase. The field's gold-standard event rule is itself defined on a 30 s window. So the >90%/95.6% figures certify event presence at coarse tolerance; they say nothing whatever about onset timing, and quoting them in a sentence about the study's precision-critical measurement is a category error. The proposed remedy — back-dating by change-point detection on the electrodermal inflection — is a good idea and an entirely unevidenced one: no source in this proposal reports the achievable precision of wrist electrodermal onset localisation against any reference, and the draft's own check (dispersion of intervals between peripheral markers) measures agreement between markers, not error against the true onset, and is completely blind to systematic lag. Systematic lag is the dangerous mode: it rotates the estimated preferred phase rather than shrinking it, at 7.2 degrees per second against a 50 s cycle, so a 12.5 s back-dating bias moves a true fragility peak onto the boundary and 25 s inverts the label. The directional prediction at L355-357 therefore requires the onset estimate to be unbiased to within about ±6 s, and nothing in the proposal can establish that. Worse, the 12.5 s figure is the most favourable possible: the filter band admits periods down to 25 s, so a participant at 0.04 Hz has a quarter-cycle tolerance of 6.25 s, and the draft never says what happens to her.
    Because the ISF cycle is only about 50 s, onset uncertainty translates directly into phase uncertainty.
  • Major (L271-274.) Both papers cited here as feasibility support report the opposite of what the design needs, and the statistic quoted is close to the wrong statistic. Lazar et al. found the infraslow sigma oscillation most prominent centro-parieto-occipitally and specifically lowest at frontopolar sites; Lecci et al.'s human recordings were C3/C4. The ZMax records F7-Fpz and F8-Fpz — bilateral frontopolar, the one region where the cited evidence is weakest. Citing the paper that documents the topographic problem as evidence that the problem does not exist is the kind of thing a specialist reviewer checks first. Separately, a bias in epoch-averaged relative band power is a static offset, and a constant offset in log sigma is removed entirely by the band-pass filter; the quantity that matters is the temporal fidelity of the sigma envelope at 0.02 Hz, on which that validation is silent. (It is also not the smallest bias of any band — gamma's is smaller — and it comes from healthy 21-28 year olds, not perimenopausal women with clinical insomnia.) The proposal then concedes the whole point two sentences later at L275-276, which means the load-bearing measurement is admittedly unvalidated and the contingency at L338-344 is the likely path rather than a fallback. Since the amplitude fallback is computed from the same frontal envelope, there is no stated route by which a posteriorly expressed rhythm is recovered from a frontal-only device.
    Feasibility is supported: sigma-band power from this headband shows the smallest bias of any band against polysomnography (0.005 ± 0.012; Esfahani et al., 2023), and the infraslow modulation of sigma is established in humans (Lecci et al., 2017; Lazar et al., 2019).
  • Major (L275-276.) There is no positive control, so a null result is uninterpretable — and I am hostile to designs with that property, because they consume three years and produce nothing publishable in the more likely branch. If phase does not predict registration, the team cannot distinguish no gating from insufficient onset precision, unmeasurable frontal ISF phase, cross-device synchronisation error, detector false positives diluting the sample, or a fallback predictor that tests a different question. Every one of those yields the same null, and the proposal concedes that at least two of them are unresolved in the very sentence I am quoting. Reporting the inputs as 'feasibility outcomes' is not the same as validating the pipeline end to end, and the dispersion check in the Risks section validates peripheral marker agreement, not whether the EEG-derived phase means anything. Two positive controls are available in these exact recordings and cost nothing: recover the human infraslow sigma-to-heart-rate coupling within participant from ZMax sigma against EmbracePlus PPG (which simultaneously validates the frontal phase estimate, the cross-device synchronisation and the achievable resolution — the three things a null would otherwise be blamed on), and recover the phase distribution of spontaneous microarousals, which validates the phase estimate against an arousal outcome with no dependence on hot flashes at all. Pre-specify both, run them before outcomes are inspected, state a pre-registered equivalence bound, and commit that a null is reported as a null only if the controls pass and as a feasibility result otherwise.
    Frontal expression and achievable phase precision are themselves feasibility outcomes.
  • Moderate (L270.) This is the inclusion criterion that determines the entire analysis sample and it is defined nowhere in Data processing or Statistical analyses. The only quantitative hint is buried forty lines later in the contingencies ('relaxing the stable-bout criterion from three ISF cycles to two'), which tells me the criterion involves a bout of some length without saying whether it precedes onset, follows it, or brackets it. That choice is decisive, not cosmetic. If stability must hold after onset, then any flash producing an arousal, a stage shift or an awakening terminates its own bout and is excluded — the sample is selected on the negation of both outcomes, the arousal model has almost no outcome variance, and the registration outcome loses exactly the events that could be pressed. Since roughly 70% of nocturnal flashes are associated with an arousal, that is not a marginal loss. Because the draft prescribes zero-phase filtering and the Hilbert transform, which are non-causal, the centred reading is the natural one, so the ambiguity is not benign. If stability is assessed pre-onset only — which is the correct choice — then the phase estimate has no post-onset support and the non-causal estimator is inconsistent with it. Also unresolved in the same cascade: 'estimation window' is named as an exclusion and never defined, and 'artefact-free' has no criterion and no rater. And note the collision with the Summary's claim at L52-53 that 'every detected flash enters both analyses': it does not, and the survival rate is unstated.
    Analyses are restricted to stable (and non-artifactual) NREM.
  • Moderate (L247-249.) Training-independence is not non-circularity, and the next sentence concedes as much, which makes the two claims contradictory within one paragraph. Circularity here does not require the detector to have seen button presses. It requires only that detection probability depend on the predictor (ISF phase) and on something that also drives the outcome (autonomic response magnitude, arousal proneness). Since the primary model is fitted only to detected flashes, detection is a collider on the paths phase -> magnitude -> detection and (unmeasured arousability) -> magnitude -> detection, and conditioning on a collider induces a phase-registration association with no causal effect present. The sign of the induced bias is not predictable from the information given. The phase-dependence of sensitivity should moreover be assumed present, not merely unexcluded: heart rate is coupled to the infraslow sigma rhythm in humans, and pulse-rate features are a substantial contributor to this detector during sleep. The proposed remedy does not remove it — electrodermal activity is a sudomotor sympathetic output of the same brain-autonomic rhythm the draft itself describes at L103-105 — and dropping features voids the cited operating point, so the fallback detector has unknown sensitivity and specificity. A separate and larger threat is untouched: phase-dependent FALSE POSITIVES. A false positive has no flash to be felt, so it enters as a guaranteed zero on both outcomes; if spontaneous non-flash electrodermal excursions are themselves phase-structured (and they are concentrated in N2/N3, which the study analyses), the contaminant is correlated with the predictor and can create or mask the effect. No positive predictive value, no false-alarm rate per hour, and no candidate-event rate appears anywhere — and specificity is uninterpretable without one.
    Labelling rests on objective physiology, not self-report: the detector is never trained on button presses, which are themselves an outcome, so it cannot be circular with respect to registration.
  • Moderate (L306-309.) The mediator logic is formally correct for a total effect, and the total effect is the wrong estimand for the stated aim. 'Gating' means the same signal enjoys different access depending on brain state. A total effect of phase on registration is fully satisfied by phase making the flash larger, which is not gating at all — it is a bigger stimulus. The proposal's own Literature Review states the correct estimand and the Statistical analyses section then abandons it: L166-169 says the informative comparison is whether 'comparable events' differ in probability, and comparability is exactly what magnitude matching or adjustment delivers. So the confirmatory analysis tests a quantity the proposal's own logic declares uninformative, and the informative one is demoted to a sensitivity analysis. This is guaranteed to bite, because magnitude is known to differ between aroused and unaroused flashes. There is also a second-order problem the draft does not see: because the sample is restricted to detected flashes and detection depends on magnitude, magnitude has already been conditioned on — truncated at the detector's threshold — so the total effect in the source population is not recovered by omitting the covariate anyway. And the mediator rule is applied inconsistently: adjustment for magnitude is refused on mediator grounds while arousal, an equally post-onset mediator and by the draft's own reasoning nearly a necessary condition for the outcome, is conditioned on at L301-302.
    Flash magnitude is a mediator, not a confounder: if ISF phase modulates the size of the autonomic response, adjusting for it would bias the total effect of phase on registration.
  • Moderate (L197-199.) The 222 is a recruitment target, not a set of women with data. It is the parent trial's planned enrolment including a 10% dropout allowance, and the draft's own next paragraph reveals that 65 have been screened. So the headline feasibility claim — the strongest sentence in the Summary — rests on a projection of a projection: a 62% eligibility rate estimated from 65 screens, applied to an accrual target roughly 30% achieved. The 137 is presented as a point estimate when the draft's own confidence interval maps to 110-161 women even at full accrual, and the interval is never propagated into anything. Nor is a recruitment rate given, which matters because the project must start between 1 January and 31 October 2027 and the draft states no start date, no duration and no schedule at all. A reviewer therefore cannot tell whether this is a retrospective analysis of data collected before the funding window, or an analysis whose accrual will still be running in 2029 — and the yield projection depends on the answer. Say what is enrolled, what has complete baseline recordings, and at what rate.
    Participants are perimenopausal women (irregular cycles and climacteric symptoms) reporting sleep disturbances, from an ongoing cohort of 222 women already being recorded.
  • Moderate (L199-200.) This is false for a substantial fraction of the sample at two of the three measurement timepoints, and the draft never says which timepoint supplies its nights. The cohort is the applicants' own four-arm randomised trial, listed under PREVIOUS OWN PUBLICATIONS at L449-454: women are allocated to transdermal estradiol plus progesterone, to online cognitive behavioural and circadian therapy for insomnia, to both, or to control, with the same device package collected at baseline, week 8 and week 15. Hormone therapy reduces vasomotor symptom frequency by roughly 75% — it does not add noise, it deletes the events the study is powered on — and it plausibly alters sigma activity, i.e. the predictor. CBT-I alters sleep continuity and arousal thresholds, i.e. also the predictor. So the omission is design-defining in two directions at once. If only the pre-randomisation block is used, say so plainly: the yield falls to one four-night block per woman, roughly a third of what 'four nights alongside seven days' plus 'an ongoing cohort of 222' invites a reader to assume, and the yield table and power calculation must be redone on that basis. If post-randomisation nights are used, treatment arm becomes a design variable requiring an arm-stratified analysis and a pre-specified arm-by-phase check, and this sentence must go. The draft resolves neither, and a reviewer who opens the cited protocol resolves it for them — which turns an analysis question into a candour question. The same omission makes 'in healthy humans and without intervention' at L369-370 indefensible as written.
    They are physically healthy and take no hormone-altering medication; other medication is documented, with attention to agents suppressing vasomotor symptoms.
  • Moderate (L355-357.) The pre-registered direction may well be backwards, and the draft commits to it in the section that will be checked against the final report. Two problems. First, the operative variable in the cited work is the SIGN OF THE DERIVATIVE, not the level: Lecci et al. report that wake-ups and sleep-throughs followed stimuli delivered during declining and rising sigma power respectively, and Osorio-Forero et al. targeted high versus low arousability by whether sigma was rising or declining, with noradrenaline peaking before sigma declines and having already declined when sigma starts to rise. Level and slope are 90 degrees apart, so defining fragility as low sigma power is a substantive misreading of the team's own paper. Second, the human evidence points the other way: the largest human characterisation of this rhythm to date reports arousal markers organised around the spindle-rich sigma peak, and human heart rate is highest at the sigma peak — explicitly opposite to mice. That paper has the draft's own named collaborator as an author and is not cited, which is the worst version of this problem: a reviewer who knows it will conclude the applicants have not read the human literature on their own predictor. The sin/cos parameterisation is direction-agnostic and survives; only the prose commits. But the prose commits in exactly the direction that the non-causal filtering artefact would produce, which means a confirmed prediction here would be the least informative possible outcome. Make the two-degrees-of-freedom test confirmatory, report the preferred phase in radians relative to the sigma maximum, and state that the direction is an open empirical question.
    Extending the exogenous literature, flashes arriving in fragility (low sigma power) are predicted to be more likely registered, and followed by an arousal, than those in continuity.
  • Moderate (L331-332, with L173, L204-206, L233-235.) The application is missing several elements the regulation makes decisive, and one of them is the section Bial states the assessment rests on. There is no section headed 'Specific Aims' — the equivalent is flowing prose under 'Research aims' with three aims embedded in sentences, none numbered, none stated as a measurable objective, none carrying a success criterion or a decision rule. There is nothing a Board member can score and nothing a final report can be checked against. There is no Host Entity or Research Centre designated anywhere (applications without one are ineligible, and the word does not appear in the document), no PI named, no CVs, no schedule against the 1 January to 31 October 2027 start window, and no budget or Euro figure of any kind — with overheads and equipment-use costs non-reimbursable and the data collection already funded by another agency. That last combination is not merely a gap: the Procedure section is written in the present tense as though the applicants run the measurement protocol, so a reviewer cannot tell whether they are being asked to pay for recruitment, devices and measurement weeks that are already paid for. The honest framing — that another funder pays for collection and this grant buys the analysis and the added measurement — is a genuinely strong argument for a small grant, and the draft never makes it. Meanwhile the single largest plausible cost, expert manual staging and arousal scoring of roughly 550 nights plus a double-scored subsample, is committed to at L233-235 and appears in no budget. And this sentence asserts completed approval with a literal placeholder, for a protocol whose primary outcome measure — the nocturnal button press — and whose tap-marker procedure do not appear in the approved parent protocol at all, and therefore require an amendment whose existence is unstated.
    The study is approved by the Medical Ethics Review Committee of Amsterdam UMC (reference [number]).
  • Minor (L287-289.) The night-within-participant random intercept is not identifiable at the achievable event density. On my own yield estimate a night contributes well under one analysable flash, so the night-level variance is informed by a small minority of nights and will sit at the boundary in a large fraction of fits — which means the model reported is not the model fitted. At these counts, and with a sparse binary outcome, the asymptotic chi-square reference for the two-degrees-of-freedom likelihood-ratio test is measurably liberal, so the nominal alpha is not the actual alpha for the single test the whole proposal turns on. This is not fatal and the fix is clean: retain only the participant random intercept, report the night term as a sensitivity analysis, and refer the confirmatory statistic to a permutation distribution obtained by shuffling ISF phase within participant, which is exact under the null and costs nothing. But the draft names the likelihood-ratio test as confirmatory inference without qualification, and at these event counts that is not a safe default. A related and unaddressed point: with only random intercepts, sin and cos are fixed effects, so the model assumes a single preferred phase and modulation depth common to every woman — while the same section concedes at L267-268 that the ISF peak frequency, and hence the phase reference itself, is estimated per participant. If preferred phases differ across women, averaging sin/cos attenuates the group effect toward zero and produces a false negative. Pre-specify participant-level random slopes on sin and cos with a stated fallback if the model is singular.
    Random intercepts are included for participant and for night within participant, with covariates for sleep stage, time since the preceding flash, and half of the night
  • Minor (L96, with L269 and L375-445.) The sigma band matches none of the cited sources, and the proposal never fixes which band the pre-registration will use. Lecci et al. used 10-15 Hz in both species; Osorio-Forero et al. used 10-15 Hz; the device validation the draft leans on defines sigma as 13-16 Hz; and the draft's own arousal criterion is >16 Hz. Four sets of band edges are in play for a quantity that IS the primary predictor, so the pre-registration cannot fix the exposure. The choice is also unfavourable in two ways at once: an 11-16 Hz upper edge abuts the arousal-defining band on the same two frontal derivations, inviting spectral leakage between predictor and outcome, and at frontal sites it maximally samples the slower frontal spindle population while the infraslow modulation is reported strongest in the fast, centro-parietal population. Fix the band, cite the source for it, leave a gap to the arousal criterion, and report at least one alternative definition as a robustness check. In the same paragraph, the sentence defining the study's central predictor names 'the IAF phase' — individual alpha frequency — which a sleep-EEG reviewer will read as either a typo for ISF or a confusion about what is being filtered, and cannot tell which. Relatedly, and cheaply fixable: Lecci et al. (2017) is cited four times as the empirical foundation of the whole rationale and does not appear in the reference list at all; Osorio-Forero et al. (2025) is cited substantively in the text and appears only under previous own publications; the 2021 reference is duplicated; one reference is formatted as a section heading; and a stray asterisk trails another. A reviewer who cannot look up the founding citation of the proposal draws a conclusion about the care taken with everything else.
    Lecci et al. (2017) described an oscillation of sigma-band (11-16 Hz) power at approximately 0.02 Hz, present in both mice and humans during NREM sleep.
  • Minor (L39-41, with L149-152.) The registration base rate that drives every power consideration in the proposal rests on a conflation, and the figure itself I could not verify in the sources provided. The 3.5-versus-1.5 contrast is between an event-level physiological count and an aggregate retrospective morning report; it does not license the inference that roughly 43% of individual flashes are registered in real time. And the primary outcome is not a morning report — it is a prospective in-night button press, which additionally requires waking enough to act, and which can diverge from recall in both directions. So the base rate underpinning the outcome balance is unknown, and it matters enormously: my calculation gives a required event count of 971 at a 43% rate and 1,867 at 15%, for the same effect size. The proposal never states which it assumed. The 20% undisturbed figure is also given as a settled quantity from the smaller of two studies (n=34) while the draft cites the larger one (n=86, 542 flashes) elsewhere without noting that it reports 29% — a difference of nearly half in the count of exactly the quiet, unaroused events the design claims as its advantage. Report the range, use the pessimistic bound for planning, give the morning diary an actual analytic job (bounding under-pressing per participant), and report power across a range of press rates rather than assuming one silently. I note the 1.5 figure does not appear in the review the draft cites for the companion 3.5 figure; verify it in the primary source or drop it.
    Women have on average 3.5 objectively recorded flashes per night but only report 1.5 (De Zambotti et al., 2014).

What would change my mind

Six specific changes, and I would move from "revise and resubmit" to "fund" on the strength of them. They are all specifiable now, without new data. (1) A yield table and a power curve, in the application. One row per exclusion — usable EEG night, onset during sleep, NREM, stable pre-onset bout, artefact-free, reliable onset — each with a retention fraction and a stated source (pilot, published estimate, or declared assumption), ending in a single expected count of analysable flashes and expected registered events, with pessimistic/central/optimistic bounds. Then name a smallest effect worth detecting (an odds ratio between best and worst phase; anchor it to the wakefulness benchmark of circular R around 0.34 rather than picking a convenient number) and report power for it across a jitter grid of 2, 5, 9 and 12.5 s, and a minimum detectable effect at the central yield. If the central yield is a few hundred flashes, as my own arithmetic suggests, then say so and reframe: make cortical arousal the primary outcome, which by my calculation carries 13.2 times the information of registration, and present registration as effect estimation plus feasibility rather than as a confirmatory test. I would fund that honest version. I will not fund a confirmatory test whose detectability the applicants have not computed. (2) A causal phase estimator, plus a negative control that can fail. Estimate ISF phase from the pre-onset log sigma envelope only — a forward-only filter or a windowed sinusoid fit on the interval ending at onset minus a stated guard — so that no post-onset EEG, no flash-related arousal, no spindle suppression and no movement artefact can enter the predictor. Quantify the bias and variance of that estimator against the non-causal one on flash-free stable NREM. Then add the control I would actually look for: recompute the primary model with phase taken from a matched epoch one full ISF cycle earlier. A true gating effect must vanish there; the artefact will not. Separate the arousal-scoring band from the predictor band, and have arousals scored by a rater blind to the sigma envelope, to the wristband channels and to the button presses — none of which the draft currently promises. (3) The estimand stated, and the hierarchy inverted. Pre-register two confirmatory tests: phase to cortical arousal among all analysable flashes (the powered replication), and phase to registration among aroused flashes, or the natural direct effect in a mediation model with arousal as mediator (the test that actually isolates conscious access). Say in one sentence that a phase effect on registration among all detected flashes is produced by arousal gating alone and is therefore not evidence about access. Resolve the inconsistency by which magnitude adjustment is refused on mediator grounds while arousal is conditioned on, and align the estimand with the aim: if the aim is gating of comparable events, the magnitude-matched contrast is the confirmatory quantity, not a sensitivity analysis. (4) Numbers on all eleven blanks, plus the twelfth. Every threshold in the Risks section and the exclusion cascade gets a value: the onset-dispersion criterion in seconds, "weak frontal ISF expression" as a spectral criterion against phase-shuffled surrogates, the low-yield trigger as an event count, the compliance floor as a rate, the maximum acceptable synchronisation residual, the artefact rule, the estimation window, the stable-bout definition (pre-onset only, in seconds and in cycles of the participant's own period), and the minimum detectable effect. Most importantly, define the primary outcome: the window within which a press counts as registering a flash, with pre-registered sensitivity analyses at two other windows, and rules for unmatched, multiply-matched and wake-period presses. And replace the amplitude fallback with a phase-preserving one — the binary sign of the sigma derivative at onset, the variable the team's own rodent work manipulated — or state plainly that amplitude tests a different hypothesis and is secondary. (5) A positive control that gates the interpretation of a null. Reproduce, within participant and before outcomes are inspected, the human infraslow sigma-to-heart-rate coupling from ZMax sigma against EmbracePlus PPG, and the phase distribution of spontaneous microarousals. Both are free in these recordings and between them they validate the frontal phase estimate, the cross-device synchronisation and the achievable resolution — the three things a null would otherwise be blamed on. Pre-commit: if the controls pass, a null is a null and is interpretable; if they fail, the study reports as a feasibility study. State an equivalence bound. A design whose null is interpretable is a fundable design; this one currently is not. (6) The timepoint, and the missing form. One sentence stating that the confirmatory analysis uses the pre-randomisation baseline block only, with the yield recomputed on that basis, and disclosing that the recordings sit inside a randomised trial of hormone therapy and CBT-I in women meeting an insomnia threshold — then arguing eligibility explicitly rather than by adjective, and dropping both "physically healthy" and "without intervention". Plus the elements the regulation requires and the document lacks entirely: a section headed Specific Aims with three numbered, falsifiable objectives; a Host Entity and named PI; CVs; a schedule with a start date inside the 2027 window; and a Euro budget that says plainly that another funder pays for collection and this grant buys the analysis, the amendment and the scoring — which is the strongest argument this application has and the one it never makes. What would NOT move me: better prose, more citations, or a promise to compute the power analysis after funding. The whole problem is that the two quantities the design turns on — expected analysable events and achievable onset precision — are deferred past the funding decision, and the one place a number does appear it is arithmetically wrong in the direction that excuses the deferral.

Menopause clinician — revise and resubmit, overall 7

Summary

This proposal asks a question I have wanted someone to ask for fifteen years. The gap between the nocturnal hot flashes women have and the ones they report is one of the oldest unresolved oddities in my field, and it has been treated almost exclusively as a measurement nuisance or a recall failure. Reframing it as a question about state-dependent access to awareness — and testing it against an endogenous, stereotyped, objectively measurable bodily event rather than an experimenter's tone — is genuinely original and squarely psychophysiological. The choice of the nocturnal flash as the model event is, in my judgement, the best available and nobody has used it this way. What is proposed to test it does not yet exist. The proposal sets its own dealbreaker at roughly 12 s of onset-timing jitter against a 50 s cycle, and there is no method in the vasomotor-symptom literature — including the one cited — that times a flash onset to anything like that resolution. The field's reference definition of a flash is a 2 µS sternal skin-conductance rise within a 30-second window; the cited detector decides in 15 s frames, computes features over windows extending ±500 s, and was scored against expert annotations within a ±90 s matching tolerance in three postmenopausal women contributing 27 laboratory flashes on a bespoke sensor array wired into a PSG amplifier. Not the study device, not the study population, not the study setting, and two orders of magnitude away from the required precision. The peripheral sudomotor inflection is also not the central event, and the latency between them has never been measured. Two further things trouble me as a clinician. The cohort is not disclosed: it is the team's own four-arm randomised trial of transdermal estradiol plus progesterone and online CBT-I in perimenopausal women meeting an insomnia threshold, and the draft calls those women "physically healthy", "with self-reported sleep disturbances", studied "without intervention". Menopausal hormone therapy reduces flash frequency by around 75% and CBT-I directly targets the symptom monitoring on which the primary outcome depends. And the analysis sample is selected on self-reported flash interference with sleep, which is the very report whose unreliability is the proposal's premise, while the analysis needs objectively detected flashes with onsets inside consolidated, arousal-free NREM — a fraction the draft's own cited review puts at well under a third of nocturnal events. No yield figure, no event count, no power figure appears anywhere. I would like to see this study run. I cannot recommend funding it in this form.

Objections raised

  • Major There is no method in the vasomotor-symptom field that can time a flash onset to the precision this design requires, and the proposal names its own dealbreaker without naming any evidence that it can be met. A quarter of a 50 s cycle is 12.5 s. The field's reference definition of a hot flash is a rise of at least 2 µS in sternal skin conductance within a 30-second period — a 30 s granularity in the criterion itself. The cited detector emits a decision every 15 s, its skin-conductance feature is defined as the ±2 minutes around a predicted onset, its temperature feature spans ±500 s, its PPG feature spans ±120 s, and it was scored against expert annotations using a ±90 s matching window. That is seven times the stated tolerance in the evaluation alone. The proposed remedy — change-point detection on the electrodermal inflection — is a good idea, but it is unvalidated, uncited, and back-dates to a peripheral sudomotor event, not to the central initiation of the flash. The latency and variability between central initiation and wrist sweat onset has never been measured; the review the applicants themselves cite reports that only 51% of detected flashes were preceded by any rise in core temperature, so the field does not even agree on what the initiating event is. This is not a detail that can be deferred to a feasibility outcome, because the entire confirmatory analysis is conditional on it.
    The binding constraint is measurement precision rather than event count: onset jitter translates directly into phase uncertainty against a 50-s cycle, and simulation shows power ceasing to improve with additional events once jitter exceeds a quarter of the cycle.
  • Major The cohort is an undisclosed randomised trial of hormone therapy and CBT for insomnia, and three separate statements in the proposal are incompatible with that. The only trace is the applicants' own protocol in the previous-publications list: a four-arm trial randomising perimenopausal women who meet an insomnia threshold to transdermal estradiol plus oral progesterone, to online cognitive behavioural and circadian therapy for insomnia, to both, or to control, with EEG and wristband recordings at three timepoints. Half the sample therefore receives hormone therapy, which the draft's own cited review reports reduces flash frequency by around 75% — that does not add noise, it removes the events the study is powered on. Calling women who meet a clinical insomnia threshold 'physically healthy' is a gloss that will not survive a reviewer opening the cited protocol, and 'in healthy humans and without intervention' in the closing paragraph is simply not true of two of four arms. The draft never states which timepoint the analysed nights come from; if it is baseline only, as the eligibility argument requires, then the available data are one four-night block per woman and the yield calculation must be redone on that basis and said out loud. As a Board member my concern here is not primarily the Article 16(6) exclusion, which I think is arguable. It is that non-disclosure converts a fit question into a candour question, and I discover the trial from the reference list rather than from the applicants.
    They are physically healthy and take no hormone-altering medication; other medication is documented, with attention to agents suppressing vasomotor symptoms.
  • Major The analysis sample is selected on the very self-report whose unreliability is the proposal's founding premise, and it is the wrong criterion for what the analysis needs. The proposal is built on the observation that women report roughly 1.5 of 3.5 objectively recorded nocturnal flashes and that a fifth to a third pass without disturbing sleep at all. It then selects participants on whether their nocturnal flashes interfere with sleep — a retrospective subjective judgement, which the cited review states is influenced by mood, expectations, body mass index and stress, and which is precisely the measure the study exists to interrogate. What the analysis actually needs is a sufficient number of objectively detected flashes whose onsets fall in consolidated, arousal-free NREM. Those two criteria come apart in exactly the direction that hurts: the women who say their flashes wake them are enriched for the aroused, remembered flashes, while the analysable events are disproportionately the quiet ones. Ambulatory monitoring in peri- and postmenopausal women gives 3.7 ± 2.2 flashes during sleeping hours with a range of 0 to 8, so a meaningful fraction of screened women will contribute no analysable nocturnal events at all. Screen on measured nocturnal flash rate from the wristband week, not on a symptom-interference question.
    The analysis sample comprises those whose nocturnal flashes interfere with sleep: of the first 65 screened, 40 (62%, 95% CI 49-72) meet this criterion, projecting to roughly 137 women.
  • Major The detection performance figures are quoted as if they were device-level validation and they are nothing of the kind, and the applicants' own senior co-author has written in print that this class of method is not ready. The source is a feasibility abstract: three women, mean age 55.6, all postmenopausal after natural menopause, one twelve-hour laboratory session in a sound-attenuated temperature-controlled bedroom, 27 flashes total, five-fold cross-validation over random 80/20 splits of 15 s frames — so training and test folds necessarily share subjects and share flashes — and an operating point produced by oversampling the flash class to a 1:2 ratio, a prevalence nothing like an overnight recording. The sensors were a custom array of discrete consumer components on the wrist cabled into a Compumedics PSG amplifier, not an integrated wristband and not the EmbracePlus. The paper's own conclusion claims 'initial feasibility'. Four transfers are being made silently at once: postmenopausal to perimenopausal, laboratory to home, bespoke wired array to a different integrated device, and a rebalanced frame-level estimate to natural overnight prevalence. And the review the draft leans on for flash physiology — co-authored by the detector's own co-author — states that such techniques 'are mostly in the development phase and have not been applied to track hot flashes in clinical trials'. A reviewer who reads both cited sources finds the proposal treating as a settled instrument the thing its own cited review calls unproven. There is also no sternal skin-conductance channel anywhere in this study, so the 90%/95.6% figures cannot be reproduced, checked or recalibrated in this sample.
    Detection follows Tsiartas et al. (2021): wrist skin conductance, temperature, pulse-rate and motion features in a decision-tree classifier, reaching over 90% sensitivity at 95.6% specificity against expert-scored sternal skin conductance, with sleep-onset performance reported separately.
  • Major There is no expected event count anywhere in the proposal, and the numbers in the applicants' own cited review make the yield small enough to change the recommendation. Six sequential exclusions are named and not one retention rate is given. Working it through on the draft's own figures and on the review it cites: 137 women × 4 baseline EEG nights × 3.5 detected flashes per night is roughly 1,900 detected events, but the follow-up analysis of the GnRH-agonist model reports that flashes occurred primarily in association with stage N1 sleep (20%) and wake epochs (51%), and de Zambotti's own cohort has 70% of flashes associated with an arousal from sleep and a further tenth occurring when the woman was already awake. Whatever the precise figure, the fraction of flash onsets falling in consolidated, arousal-free NREM is under a third. Published usable-recording rates for this headband run between roughly a half and two thirds, worse in older and clinical samples. Then apply the stable-bout requirement, the artefact criterion and the reliable-onset criterion. I land in the low hundreds of analysable flashes and perhaps a few dozen registered ones, for a two-degrees-of-freedom circular test whose effect is additionally attenuated by timing jitter. That may still be worth doing as an estimation study; it is not a confirmatory test, and the proposal must say which it is rather than promising the arithmetic after the money is spent.
    Expected yield is estimated by applying the planned exclusions sequentially - EEG night, NREM, stable NREM, estimation window, artefact-free recording, reliable onset timing.
  • Major The stable-NREM restriction and the claim that every detected flash contributes cannot both be true, and one reading of the restriction deletes the outcome. The proposal says analyses are restricted to stable, non-artefactual NREM, and the contingency section reveals that 'stable' means a bout of three infraslow cycles, relaxable to two. It never says whether that window precedes the onset, brackets it, or follows it — and since the phase estimator is a zero-phase filter plus Hilbert transform, the natural reading is that it brackets it. If stability must hold after onset, then a flash that produces an arousal, a stage shift or an awakening terminates its own bout and is excluded, which means inclusion is conditioned on the negation of both outcomes. Given that roughly 70% of nocturnal flashes are associated with an arousal and that a button press requires waking enough to act and generates a large wrist motion transient within seconds, the surviving sample would be enriched for precisely the quiet flashes on which the outcome is constant. State that the window is pre-onset only, that arousal and awakening are outcomes and never exclusion criteria, and report how many registered flashes survive each step.
    Both are fitted to every detected flash, so events passing without arousal or report contribute.
  • Major The primary outcome measure has no operational definition, is not in the parent protocol, and in this population measures attribution and arousal rather than detection. Three separate problems. First, operationally: no window is given linking a press to a detected onset, no rule for multiple presses, none for presses with no detected flash, none for presses during scored wake, none for press latency. A flash lasts one to five minutes; a woman may wake, orient, become aware she is hot, and press minutes later or at a later awakening. Against a 50 s cycle, plausible latencies exceed a full cycle, and latency will itself vary with depth of sleep, which is the predictor. Different defensible windows produce different confirmatory results from the same data. Second, construct: pressing 'as soon as she thinks she is having a flash' requires her to wake, notice she is hot, and causally attribute the sensation to a flash rather than to the room, the duvet, or the insomnia. In a cohort selected for insomnia and for flash-related sleep disturbance, that attribution is exactly where expectancy operates — the review notes a significant placebo response for reported flashes — and the amplitude of skin conductance does not represent self-reported severity, so the objective and subjective channels are not two views of one quantity. Third, and worst for a nested design: instructing women to monitor for and report flashes is itself an intervention on symptom monitoring, and one arm of the parent trial receives CBT-I, whose explicit target is reducing nocturnal symptom monitoring and sleep-related arousal. The therapy perturbs the outcome instrument. The design already contains an unused control for reactivity — three wristband nights without the button-press instruction.
    On EEG nights participants press a wristband button as soon as they think they are having a flash; this time-stamped press is a prospective measure of conscious registration.
  • Moderate The closing clinical claim is uncited, one-sided, and the evidence that would actually support it is sitting in the review the applicants cite. The claim that treating flashes does not reliably resolve the sleep complaint is contradicted on page 110 of Gombert-Labedens et al., which states that the flash–sleep link 'is further supported by studies showing that the treatment of hot flashes ... with hormone therapy reduces sleep disturbances'. But nine pages later the same review reports that fezolinetant reduced vasomotor symptom frequency by around 61% with no significant improvement in patient-reported sleep disturbance at week 12. So the literature is genuinely mixed and the applicants have cited only the half that undercuts them while omitting the half that supports them. Two consequences. Scientifically, an uncited claim contradicted by one's own reference is the cheapest possible loss of reviewer trust. Clinically, I object to the framing on its own terms: implying to a general readership that treating vasomotor symptoms does not help menopausal sleep is not what the evidence says, and under-treatment of vasomotor symptoms is already a real harm in my clinic. And to this funder specifically, ending a psychophysiology proposal on a treatment-efficacy claim invites the very therapy exclusion the rest of the document is trying to stay clear of. Delete the therapeutic sentence and end on the mechanism.
    It would also give a mechanistic account of a clinical puzzle - why women report far fewer nocturnal hot flashes than they have, and why treating the flashes does not reliably resolve the sleep complaint that accompanies them.
  • Moderate Bedroom temperature is absent from a home study of thermoregulatory events, and the applicants cite the paper that establishes why it matters — twice — without mentioning it. The reference they give is titled 'Effects of REM sleep AND AMBIENT TEMPERATURE on hot flash-induced sleep disturbance'. Half of that paper is about ambient temperature, and cooling the bedroom reduces nocturnal flash count, with the effect concentrated in the first half of the night. Ambient temperature also raises tonic skin conductance directly, so it moves the detector's principal input and its false-positive rate, and it interacts with the known problem of sweat accumulating under a wrist device during immobile deep sleep. Recording is at home, unsupervised, across seasons, with bedding, sleepwear, heating, open windows and bed-sharing unrecorded. This is the largest uncontrolled source of variance in both event supply and detection specificity, and it is the cheapest to fix: a bedside temperature and humidity logger costs almost nothing and imposes no participant burden. Enter mean and within-night bedroom temperature as covariates, add a temperature-by-half-of-night term, and record bedding and bed-sharing in the morning diary.
    The design is within-subject, observational and multi-night, conducted at home.
  • Moderate The thermophysiology in the mechanistic paragraph will not survive a specialist reading, on terminology and on certainty. The cited review devotes a paragraph to ruling explicitly that 'thermoneutral zone' denotes the zone between ambient-temperature thresholds, while the zone between core-temperature thresholds — the one hypothesised to narrow in symptomatic women — is the inter-threshold zone. The draft uses the term the review specifically sets aside, in the sentence where it summarises that review. The projection target is also incomplete: the review names both the median preoptic nucleus and the medial preoptic area. And the narrowing is stated as fact where the source calls the evidence mixed: only 51% of detected flashes were preceded by any rise in gastrointestinal temperature, mild heating producing far larger core rises did not reliably provoke a flash, and sweating thresholds were similar in symptomatic postmenopausal and young premenopausal individuals. The review's own abstract flags 'the mixed research findings about thresholds for sweating in symptomatic individuals'. Separately, the following sentence attributes noradrenergic input specifically to the median preoptic nucleus on the authority of a preoptic review that discusses the ventrolateral preoptic area and projection-defined populations, and that never mentions KNDy neurons, oestrogen or hot flashes at all. That swap is the load-bearing step in the 'single infraslow rhythm times arousability and thermoeffector drive together' argument, and it is a conjecture dressed as a citation. The stronger and genuinely relevant evidence is in the review already: yohimbine provokes flashes, clonidine ameliorates them, so central noradrenergic tone is implicated in flash initiation on pharmacological grounds. Use that instead.
    Oestrogen withdrawal hyperactivates arcuate KNDy neurons, which signal through the neurokinin 3 receptor to the median preoptic nucleus and narrow the thermoneutral zone (Gombert-Labedens et al., 2025).
  • Moderate The flash–arousal ordering reversal is stated as established fact and used to justify a model covariate, while the draft's own other citation reports no such difference. The review the applicants rely on describes this as one finding among conflicting ones: one study found awakenings more likely before than after a flash, another found flashes preceding awakenings only in the first half of the night, and others found flashes and awakenings largely coincident with no difference between halves — the last of these being de Zambotti et al. 2014, which the draft cites twice for its headline prevalence figures. A further study found 80% of flashes occurring before or concurrently with an awakening with a similar pattern in both halves. Keeping half-of-night as a covariate is fine; asserting the reversal as settled while citing, in the same document, the paper that contradicts it is not. More substantively, if arousal frequently precedes the flash then the causal arrow in the supporting aim is reversed and cortical arousal becomes a cause of detection rather than a consequence of the flash — a threat to the central logic that goes unaddressed. Report the sign and distribution of the arousal-to-onset interval, and pre-specify how flashes whose onset closely follows an arousal are handled.
    Freedman and Roehrs (2006) showed that hot flashes are suppressed during REM sleep, when thermoregulatory effector responses are largely inactive, and that the flash-arousal ordering reverses across the night: flashes precede arousals in the first half, arousals precede flashes in the second.
  • Moderate The mediator reasoning is formally right and selects the wrong estimand, and the magnitude proxy is known not to track what it is being asked to proxy. The rule cited is correct for a total effect, but a total effect is not what the proposal says it wants: the aims promise to separate gating of peripheral flash expression from gating of cortical and conscious registration, and the literature review states that 'the informative comparison for conscious gating is whether, among flashes that do occur, comparable events have different probabilities'. Comparability is exactly what magnitude adjustment or matching delivers. So the confirmatory analysis tests a quantity the proposal's own stated logic calls uninformative, and the analysis that would be informative is demoted to a sensitivity check. This matters because magnitude is not balanced across the outcome: flashes associated with arousal or awakening are accompanied by larger heart-rate and blood-pressure increases than flashes in undisturbed sleep, so the unadjusted contrast is partly a magnitude contrast by construction. A positive total effect driven entirely by phase making the flash bigger would satisfy the confirmatory test while contradicting the headline interpretation that an infraslow rhythm sets when an internal event becomes an experience. Two caveats I would want stated: skin-conductance amplitude does not represent self-reported flash severity, so magnitude must be a multivariate index rather than one number; and because the sample is restricted to detected flashes, magnitude has already been truncated at the detector's threshold before any model is fitted.
    Flash magnitude is a mediator, not a confounder: if ISF phase modulates the size of the autonomic response, adjusting for it would bias the total effect of phase on registration.
  • Moderate The directional prediction the proposal commits to is not the one its sources support, and the human data point the other way. Fragility in the cited rodent work is defined by the sign of the sigma derivative, not the level: wake-ups followed stimuli delivered during declining sigma and sleep-throughs during rising sigma, and the thalamic noradrenaline measurements show noradrenaline rising before sigma declines and already declined when sigma starts to rise, giving a non-symmetrical U-shaped course. So the high-noradrenaline, high-arousability window sits at and just after the sigma peak, not in the trough. Mapping fragility onto low sigma power is a substantive misreading of the applicants' own paper. The human literature compounds it: the largest human characterisation of this rhythm places microarousal markers around the spindle-rich peak, and human heart rate is highest at the sigma peak, explicitly opposite to mice. The sin/cos parameterisation is direction-agnostic and survives all of this — only the prose commits. But the Expected Outcomes paragraph pre-registers a direction that the primary sources do not support in that form, and a reviewer who knows this literature will read it as evidence the human work on the predictor has not been read. Restate the phases as rising versus declining sigma and make the direction an empirical question.
    Extending the exogenous literature, flashes arriving in fragility (low sigma power) are predicted to be more likely registered, and followed by an arousal, than those in continuity.
  • Moderate The one contingency protecting the study's acknowledged principal risk substitutes a different hypothesis and calls it the same one, and it fails in the same conditions it is meant to rescue. Phase and amplitude answer different questions. The primary claim is that when within an endogenous cycle an interoceptive event arrives determines whether it reaches awareness — a claim about temporal alignment, and the reason the design is interesting is that phase is orthogonal to mean sleep depth within a bout. Pre-flash amplitude asks whether registration is more likely when the rhythm is strongly expressed, a state-level question heavily confounded with N2 versus N3, spindle density, homeostatic pressure and time of night — the very confounds the phase design exists to escape.
